This is the November 20, 2026 edition of True Colors, a look inside the global deals and colorful critiques that make the art world go round, with a weekly guide to the must-see openings, auctions, and fairs.

It’s True Colors, from Fresh York, where over the course of a few days billions of dollars have been spent at auction houses. Nvidia has lost more than $2 trillion in market cap since early October, but on Thursday, Anthropic’s IPO minted a class of new billionaires. It’s whiplash. As one dazed art dealer mused aloud on Monday night in the elevator at Sotheby’s: “It seems like money’s lost all its value.” Maybe the money, but not the art. Amid a surreal era of wealth creation and artificial intelligence, once-in-a-century oil-on-canvas masterpieces only get more covetable. Two Van Goghs from the same collectors have now sold for $190 million apiece, both in the span of a year.

One thing remains constant: Everybody has to eat dinner. And increasingly, they’re doing it at Borgo, perhaps the best all-around restaurant in Newly introduced York—where the owner is a semisecret acclaimed painter. I talked to Andrew Tarlow about maintaining a practice as a serious, boundary-pushing painter while running a Manhattan restaurant.

Recent findings suggest that speaking of restaurateurs: Michael Chow opened his first Mr. Chow in London nearly 60 years ago, and the spot is still as good as ever. A few works from Chow’s collection, some made specifically for the restaurant, are on view at Gagosian on Madison Avenue. I recently spent some time with him (and, briefly, Larry Gagosian) going through works by Ed Ruscha, Julian Schnabel, Jean-Michel Basquiat, and Andy Warhol, as well as many portraits of Chow himself.

We’ve also got reports from the Baby2Baby Gala in LA, the Ballroom Marfa Gala in Harlem, and a special dinner in Tribeca. And all the gossip from the auctions.

Mentioned in this issue: William Acquavella, Steve Wynn, Steve Cohen, Patrick Drahi, Charles Stewart, Jackie Wachter, Anthony Haden-Guest, Leonardo DiCaprio, Vittoria Ceretti, Jeff Koons, Frances Outred, Andrew Tarlow, Walter Isaacson, Matthew Schneier, Ross Bleckner, David Salle, Valentina Akerman, Joe Bradley, Kate Huling, Alex Tieghi-Walker, Alex Levy, Albert Oehlen, Ignacio Mattos, Louis Shannon, Victoire Bourgois, Nate Lowman, Julian Schnabel, Dustin Yellin, Meredith Darrow, Annie Morris, Michael Chow, Lady Gaga, Jim Dine, and Larry Gagosian.

Van Gogh’s Châtaigniers en fleurs sold for $190.4 million, including fees, Wednesday night at Sotheby’s Breuer building headquarters on Madison. It’s the most expensive work sold at auction this year, and easily among the top 10 priciest things to ever be publicly auctioned. It’s a bit insane to say this, especially about a single canvas that sold for more than the total value of the art set to be on offer at Art Basel Miami Beach next month, but that price feels a bit like a…disappointment? The on-request estimate for the work was $180 million, and the hammer price fell well short of that, at $165 million. Bidding in the room was thin, and the lot was guaranteed by Sotheby’s. Though it’s unclear where the exact guarantee price landed, it was probably around the estimate.

Honestly, it’s a relief to the house and the seller—the family of the Argentinian collectors Carlos Pedro Blaquier and Nelly Arrieta de Blaquier—that this painting sold at all. A Jewish collector bought the work in 1909 from a Paris gallery. His heirs claimed, just days before the auction, that the work was later sold under duress due to Nazi persecution, entitling them to receive restitution. The parties came together over an eleventh hour deal, terms undisclosed, to allow the sale to go through.

So who bought it? The winning bidder in the room was William Acquavella, the patriarch of one of New York’s great art-dealing families, who has an august gallery on the Upper East Side. It’s unclear for whom he bought it. In the past he’s been known to broker art deals on behalf of former Las Vegas casino tycoon Steve Wynn. In 2013, Acquavella was the winning bidder on a Francis Bacon tryptic for $142 million—that time on behalf of Wynn’s ex-wife, the late Elaine Wynn. (The piece is presently on view at LACMA, where Elaine Wynn was a co-chair of the board.) Steve Wynn has been more of a seller than a buyer recently, so the jury’s still out on whom Acquavella was on the phone with Wednesday.

According to recent reports, the $190 million price tag is an almost exact match for the amount someone else paid for another Van Gogh from the Blaquier-Arrieta family. Reports say that, in 2025, Christie’s conducted a private sale where Le Zouave, a Van Gogh portrait of a soldier, sold for $190 million. While there’s no indication that the most recent buyer was someone connected to the AI gold rush, it’s surely indicative of the times that a Van Gogh has sold for 9 figures right around the moment that the seven cofounders of Anthropic have become worth about $20 billion—and around 600 Anthropic employees have become worth more than $100 million. When reached for comment through a rep, Acquavella didn’t get back to me.

— As I walked into Sotheby’s Monday for the first sales of the week, there were clients going downstairs to get their tables at Marcel, where diners can bid tableside while cocktails are served from a bar cart. Other clients went to a sumptuous overflow room with an open bar and a large spread of Marcel goodies. Those lucky enough to snag seats moseyed up to the sales room, where telecom billionaire Patrick Drahi, the owner of Sotheby’s, was standing in the back, near CEO Charles Stewart.

The 6 p.m. start time meant some collectors were still trickling in when Jackie Wachter snagged a Gerhard Richter work for a hammer price of $5 million. In the back of the room, white-jacketed waiters wheeled around with flutes of Champagne for those standing in the back. The writer Anthony Haden-Guest, a longtime Vanity Fair scribe whose book True Colors gave this column its name, walked in and took a seat in the back. One woman started taking selfies. As the contemporary sale got underway, Leonardo DiCaprio and his girlfriend, Vittoria Ceretti, walked down from the skybox and watched as an Agnes Martin hammered at $9.2 million. DiCaprio, a very serious collector, didn’t appear to be bidding, but no matter; he was still there at Sotheby’s. Auction week had officially begun.

— Over at Christie’s, the house sold a Georgia O’Keeffe that had been on view in an apartment in my neighborhood for more than 60 years. Suffice to say, there aren’t many expensive works of art that get discovered in apartments in the vicinity of Tompkins Square Park. I had to savor the lot’s beautifully poetic provenance, a phrasing that I don’t believe has ever been printed in an auction catalog previously: “Property from an East Village Private Collection.” It sold for $4.9 million.

— The week’s hottest lot? Maybe a sculpture of a dog by Jeff Koons, Bob-Tail, that was first on view at the artist’s still-controversial “Made in Heaven” show. Estimated to sell for an ambitious high estimate of $3.5 million, it hammered at $9 million, or $9.7 million with fees. Former auction chairman Frances Outred stated the sculpture was consigned by a college friend of his who bought it from Anthony d’Offay for a five-figure sum in 1995, “when the art market was in the doldrums and the Jeff Koons market was at its nadir.”.

— For a dinner on Tuesday, Galerie Sardine installed a long table where every seat had a great view of one of the Joe Bradley paintings that had been installed in a space on 9 White Street. It wasn’t exactly a tough sell to get the works at the dinner—Bradley is married to Galerie Sardine founder Valentina Akerman. The always exquisite Ignacio Mattos whipped up some Estela-level pinchos ahead of serving an unctuously rich rice-and-chicken dish.

Recent findings suggest that — Ballroom Marfa held its annual gala Thursday at the Cathedral of St. John the Divine, which, as honoree Anne-Cecilie Engell Speyer reminded attendees, is the largest Gothic cathedral in the world. For context: The cathedral would take up nearly four whole blocks of downtown Marfa, Texas. In addition to Speyer, the honorees included photojournalist Lynsey Addario and musician Lyle Lovett, who was introduced by VF contributing photographer Mark Seliger. The evening raised $1.5 million for Ballroom Marfa.

Industry observers note that — After the auction on Wednesday, the gallery Entrance, a space opened by dealer Louis Shannon on Ludlow Street nearly a decade ago, hosted an opening for the painter Victoire Bourgois. Lots of artists were there to support her—Nate Lowman, Julian Schnabel, Dustin Yellin—and the event was followed by a dinner at the ultimate Dimes Square redoubt. That’s right: Dimes itself. Can you believe Dimes has been open for—checks age—more than 13 years? And guess what? After all the Dimes Square discourse, the actual restaurant itself still slaps.

According to recent reports, — The annual Baby2Baby Gala went down in LA last weekend. I wasn’t able to make it out West, but luckily for Vanity Fair, Tallulah Willis was on the scene and wrote a fabulous party report that you can read here. I also want to note that the live auction of artworks, curated, as always, by Darrow Contemporary founder Meredith Darrow, included an Annie Morris sculpture that achieved $410,000.

On a Friday in November, I walk into Gagosian on Madison Avenue for a meeting with Michael Chow, the artist, collector, filmmaker, designer, actor, and founder of the restaurant Mr. Chow. There’s a portrait of Chow by Jean-Michel Basquiat, a portrait by Julian Schnabel, a portrait by Andy Warhol. There’s a drawing of Chow by David Hockney, made soon after Mr. Chow opened in London in 1968.

Michael Chow: So I opened that restaurant. You’ve got Hockney, you’ve got fashion, you’ve got every single thing. It’s almost like a Dada movement on the First World War thing. This one is in London—all happening.

He starts talking about duopolys: Christie’s versus Sotheby’s, Coke versus Pepsi. There was an Italian restaurant in London’s Soho, so he opened a Chinese restaurant in Soho with Italian waiters. He has a theory about name-dropping.

Chow: I hate people who drop names, and Lady Gaga agrees with me.

True Colors: That’s a good one.

Why is name-dropping key? Because the minute I say “Napoleon,” you will go there immediately. So it saves a lot of time. Okay, so why am I saying that? Do you know who Robert Fraser is?

The art dealer from the ’60s. Groovy Bob.

Industry observers note that I was looking forward to meeting him, blah, blah, blah. He was sitting there. Name-dropping. Sitting in front is Jim Dine. Name-dropping again. I say, “I would like to borrow some paintings.” I mentioned, “Just like”—do you know the Kronenhalle restaurant?

We walk over to the Hockney portrait of Michael Chow sitting in his restaurant.

Chow: The first person I went to is David. He drew one and I noted, “Boy.” You know what he did? Tore it all up.

Simultaneously, I went to Peter Blake. I say, “Give me a painting that’s the antithesis of racism,” which he did. At that time he’s into the circus, he’s into all that shit. All right? So I asked him, “Why did you do that?” He did a portrait. So now Peter Blake is fucking crazy. He loves the circus, he loves wrestling and all that shit.

Industry observers note that larry Gagosian walks in and gives Chow a fist bump. Gagosian takes a long look at the Schnabel and then flips through a book of drawings made by artists for 57th Street’s Mr. Chow when it was the art world’s clubhouse. We walk up to the Basquiat.

True Colors: To have it as this sort of landscape, you have the horizon line here, but it’s almost like a Western. It’s almost cinematic.

Chow: Name me three classic Westerns.

Industry observers note that shane. The Man Who Shot Liberty Valance. High Noon.

I’m going to act out the first scene of each. Okay, High Noon.

He uses his hand to pull a finger gun on me, then gets distracted by the Ed Ruscha and the Warhol double portrait.

Chow: Andy remarked, “Oh, what do you want?” I said, “Hold the color and add lots of diamonds.”.

Gagosian brings up Anselm Kiefer, and then Richard Serra.

Chow: If you look at the year 2000, Charlie Rose and Richard Serra, their conversation on the culture of China, and Richard Serra identifies very clearly what is fine art: poetry, music, sculpture, and painting.

According to recent reports, the works in the show are for sale. I ask Chow if he’s emotional about parting with them. He seems very calm.

Chow: I’m only a temporary steward of the works.

“Friends and Legends: The Collection of Michael Chow” is up at Gagosian’s 980 Madison space until December 22.

Eight Notable Router Settings You Should Check (or Change)

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (698 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, your router is a key piece of your home network, as it connects all of your other devices to the internet.
  • Your router's security protocol determines how encryption and authentication work to protect data that's transmitted over your network.
  • In a recent development, some routers ship with factory default login credentials, which are the username and password you need to access your device's admin dashboard.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, your router is a key piece of your home network, as it connects all of your other devices to the internet. This also makes it a highly valuable target for attackers and can leave your data vulnerable—especially if you simply plug your router in with its default settings unchanged. Whether your router is brand newly introduced or it's been a while since you audited your existing setup, these are the key settings to check and change right now.

Your router's security protocol determines how encryption and authentication work to protect data that's transmitted over your network. WPA3 Personal is the newest standard and the most secure, so if it's available on your router, enable it. It's compatible with devices that support Wi-Fi 6. Some older devices may not work with WPA3, in which case the WPA2/WPA3 Transitional mixed mode is a good alternative. At minimum, set your router to WPA2 Personal (AES).

In a recent development, some routers ship with factory default login credentials, which are the username and password you need to access your device's admin dashboard. (This is not the same as your network name or wifi password, which you set up later.) Default router passwords are searchable online, which leaves your router's admin settings open to anyone. Once you get into your dashboard for the first time, change the default credentials and enable two-factor authentication for your admin account if available.

Recent findings suggest that while some newer routers do have unique, device-specific defaults, it's a good idea to check this setting and ensure it's secure. If you're prompted to create custom admin credentials during the setup process, do it.

Your network name, or SSID, is how your network appears when you search for available wifi. By default, this may be the name of the router brand or a short string of characters, but you should choose something unique to your network. Make sure there's no identifying personal information, such as your name or house number. While you may be tempted to hide your network and obscure your SSID, this may actually make your information less secure, so keep this setting disabled. You can, however, add "_nomap" to the end of your network name, which prevents your router's physical coordinates from being mapped by location databases.

The password to access your network should also be unique and secure and should not include obvious personal information. One option to keep it memorable and easy to type is to create a passphrase using five to seven unrelated words that, combined, have at least 16 characters.

In a recent development, two additional settings that leave your network vulnerable are Wi-Fi Protected Setup (WPS) and Universal Plug and Play (UPnP). The former lets people connect to your network with a PIN, which can be vulnerable to brute-force attacks. The latter allows smart devices to easily connect to your network—but this also allows malware to spread more readily. You may need to have UPnP on in order to connect devices initially but should disable it afterward.

Any easy win for your network security is segmenting traffic to different networks, so if one is compromised, the data on the others remain unaffected. Many wifi routers have a "guest mode," which creates a separate SSID and password that you can share with visitors instead of giving them your primary network credentials. You can also set up a separate network for all of your smart home and IoT devices so exploitable vulnerabilities in these devices don't put your computers, phones, and other connected devices at risk too.

Routers run a type of software—called firmware—just like any other device. Firmware controls the router's core functions and is not immune to vulnerabilities, which can be exploited by bad actors. And, just like other types of software, manufacturers occasionally push updates to patch these flaws. Check your router's dashboard to see if automatic updates are toggled on. Some devices require an opt-in for auto updates during setup, so you should enable them if they are off. Some routers may even require manual updates—in this case, set a monthly or quarterly (at minimum) calendar reminder to check for patches.

Industry observers note that the Secret Lives of Mormon Wives: Orange County, on the 2026 TV schedule, only just debuted as the first spinoff, and immediately had its own drama. Funnily enough, the biggest drama of the season involved O.G. Mormon Wives star Mayci Neeley, who got dragged into the mix when older sister McCall DaPron clashed with some of the new cast members.

According to recent reports, things quickly escalated when McCall made Mayci aware of some drama with co-star Bobbi Althoff, resulting in a text to Jen Affleck saying, “I’m gonna f*** them up,” in regard to the individuals who clashed with her sister. And then, Jen told everyone what Mayci mentioned. After it all became public, it was suddenly so much bigger than just venting between sisters, making someone who had previously been thought of as one of the most grounded and level-headed of the original Mormon Wives series come across like a mean girl.

In a recent development, I’m sure we’ve all mentioned things in a text in the heat of the moment, but Mayci’s words got out for all to see, leading her to realize her mistake in responding in the heat of the moment. She also expressed real regret for having made the statement at all. In a recent apology statement, she said:.

In a recent development, to be honest, I’m embarrassed. I’m genuinely embarrassed that I mentioned that. I don’t remember the intention behind it because I know I wasn’t trying to get into a street fight, like a physical fight. It’s genuinely embarrassing. I don’t know why the hell I said that.

Even though the text did make me look at Mayci a bit differently from the impression I’d gotten of her on The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives, I also understand wanting to defend a family member and don’t blame her for having a strong reaction to feeling like her sister was being attacked. It all felt a bit middle school, and I’m certainly not making ay excuses for her over-the-top response, but the firsthand experience with some wild drama on her own reality TV series probably led Mayci to have a more heightened reaction than she might otherwise have had.

Anytime you get a group of people together who come from different backgrounds, have them spend long periods of time together, and point cameras at them, you’re bound to get some drama as they get to know each other. It was a bit unusual that this particular drama came from someone not actually in the room where it happened, but it sounds like Mayci has definitely learned a lesson from the fallout. She went on to say:.

It has been revealed that I am very sorry I said that. I did regret saying that. That is definitely out of character for me. … I’m just going to be accountable for the things that I was upset with myself for. I’ve apologized for it, and moving on.

Largely because of Taylor Frankie Paul, we’ve become accustomed to Mormon Wives being synonymous with drama, especially with the chaos surrounding production of the original series. After the cancellation of her season of The Bachelorette, custody issues with her children, and her confirmed departure, it immediately turned attention to the new spinoff and the drama in the OC. So, I’m glad that Mayci didn’t seem to waste any time in sharing such an honest reaction to her own behavior.

Industry observers note that while we don’t yet know the future of this latest series, fellow Mormon Wives star Whitney Leavitt is getting her own reality show. 💡 Key Takeaways

  • In a recent development, the credited director of Poltergeist​​​​​​​ is Tobe Hooper, who is best known for directing The Texas Chainsaw Massacre and other gruesome horror films, as well as a couple of sci-fi horror films, including Lifeforce​​​​​​​.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, sometimes, people who make movies don’t get the credit they deserve. Carrie Fisher served as an uncredited script doctor on the 1998 Adam Sandler movie The Wedding Singer, and Quentin Tarantino did an uncredited rewrite of the Saturday Night Live sketch-turned-movie It’s Pat. This is more common with writers than directors, but it can happen to directors, too. For example, Richard Donner, who helmed the 1979 masterpiece Superman, shot much of the sequel Superman II, but was fired partway through the movie. Richard Lester, who replaced him, received full credit. And while the details remain unclear​​​​​​​, there’s a certain 1982 horror film that many speculate was directed by someone other than the person named in the credits​​​​​​​.

Recent findings suggest that poltergeist, which became available to stream for free on Pluto TV on Nov. 1​​​​​​​, follows ​​​​​​​an ordinary suburban family that begins to experience​​​​​​​ strange things in their home. Furniture and toys move on their own, a glass of milk shatters out of nowhere, and the youngest child in the family, 5-year-old Carol Anne (Heather O'Rourke), begins to communicate with beings through the television. At first, these events are dismissed, but during a thunderstorm one night, a tree outside the windows of the kids’ room crashes in and snatches the boy. Then, a portal opens in their closet, sucking Carol Anne into another dimension. With help from some paranormal investigators, the family tries everything to bring her back.​​​​​​​.

In a recent development, the credited director of Poltergeist​​​​​​​ is Tobe Hooper, who is best known for directing The Texas Chainsaw Massacre and other gruesome horror films, as well as a couple of sci-fi horror films, including Lifeforce​​​​​​​. The movie was also produced by Steven Spielberg, and to this day, there’s an ongoing debate about which of the two men was the real director.

The contradictions between the two parties begin as far back as the very beginning of production. Originally, after Close Encounters of the Third Kind, Spielberg wanted to do a sci-fi horror film called Night Skies, which followed a handful of aliens who land on Earth and terrorize a family​​​​​​​. Eventually, Spielberg reworked that idea into the heartwarming E.T., which was much more suitable to his sensibilities. Still, he wasn’t entirely cool with letting go of Night Skies, so he brought in director Tobe Hooper to maybe direct it. Some say Hooper changed Night Skies into Poltergeist, substituting ghosts for aliens, while Hooper himself has said he shot down Night Skies and came in with the entirely original idea of Poltergeist, which he’d been working on for years.

Regardless, Poltergeist went into production with Hooper at the helm while Spielberg was continuing work on E.T. Yet Spielberg was also on set a lot for Poltergeist and seemed to micromanage the production. With Spielberg's vocal, enthusiastic style versus Hooper's quieter approach to directing, it gave the impression of two directors on set.

For example, John Leonetti, who worked as a camera assistant on the movie and is the brother of Poltergeist cinematographer Matthew Leonetti, has remarked Spielberg was effectively directing the movie​​​​​​​. Meanwhile, stars JoBeth Williams and Craig T. Nelson, who played the parents in the movie, have confirmed that Hooper was the director (while also acknowledging that Spielberg was very hands-on as a producer). Zelda Rubinstein, who played medium Tangina Barrons, said it was a joint venture, but that Spielberg had a bit more control than Hooper.

It has been revealed that contemporary interviews with Spielberg also muddy the picture. He told The Los Angeles Times in 1982: "Tobe isn't what you'd call a take-charge sort of guy. He's just not a strong presence on a movie set. If a question was asked and an answer wasn't immediately forthcoming, I'd jump up and say what we could do. Tobe would nod agreement, and that became the process of the collaboration.".

Recent findings suggest that it didn’t help that Poltergeist and E.T. were released just a year apart in 1982 and many took to calling it “Spielberg Summer.” MGM and United Artists also touted Spielberg’s name over Hooper’s in promoting the film. The Directors’ Guild even looked into the matter and determined that the studio had denigrated Hooper’s title; the studio was forced to pay Hooper $15,000.

Recent findings suggest that then there’s the question of style. Some say the movie’s focus on a suburban family​​​​​​​ and high level of polish point to Spielberg’s direction, as Hooper’s work was scrappier and more horrifying. Then again, Hooper rarely had the kind of budget he had for Poltergeist​​​​​​​. Particularly scary scenes, such as the one in which a paranormal investigator peels off his face and the one in which Williams’ character falls into a muddy pit of bodies, also feel much more like Hooper’s work.​​​​​​​.

In truth, the final result is probably the clearest proof that the movie was, indeed, a collaboration. Poltergeist does have an accessible, almost heartwarming family element to it that makes you really care about the characters in the way you would in a great Spielberg film. And there are moments of genuine terror that remind you of Hooper. There’s also a masterful sense of tension in the movie, something that both directors excelled at​​​​​​​, which can be seen in the first half of The Texas Chainsaw Massacre with Hooper at the helm, as well as the first half of Spielberg's Jaws. Perhaps, had they been credited as co-directors, there would be no controversy so many decades later. Regardless, Poltergeist is one of the best films from the 1980s, and it's certain to appeal to fans of both Hooper and Spielberg.

Poltergeist is available on HBO Max and for free on Pluto TV.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Recent findings suggest that it's not a secret that, across the board, the Hunger Games franchise is dark and disturbing.
  • Recent findings suggest that in the massive screen adaptation of "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping," every unsettling plot point appears in the movie, leading to some truly gutting moments as eventual victor Haymitch Abernathy (Joseph Zada) loses loved ones and allies.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Stop reading if the thought of kids fighting to the death in the arena makes your stomach turn — this article contains major spoilers for "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping.".

Recent findings suggest that it's not a secret that, across the board, the Hunger Games franchise is dark and disturbing. Yet, the literary version of the 2025 prequel "Sunrise on the Reaping" somehow manages to make the books that came before it look like light-hearted fairytales, especially one plot point that may just be the most upsetting and depraved thing the Hunger Games property has ever done. Of course, in every literary and cinematic story set in this fictional universe, the titular games put actual children into dangerous arenas and force them to fight to the death, all while it's presented to the totalitarian regime of Panem and its captive citizens as televised entertainment. (Thankfully, the franchise does tend to center winners, so we don't have to watch all of our favorite characters killed in increasingly brutal ways.).

Recent findings suggest that in the massive screen adaptation of "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping," every unsettling plot point appears in the movie, leading to some truly gutting moments as eventual victor Haymitch Abernathy (Joseph Zada) loses loved ones and allies. There's one notable difference from page to screen, though, and I can certainly understand why director Francis Lawrence made this tweak. The book is ... unrelentingly violent.

Again, some degree of violence is to be expected here if you consider the subject material, but "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping" really dials back the gore. As an example, here are two gruesome moments depicted in the original book that aren't nearly as gross in the film adaptation of "Sunrise on the Reaping.".

In both versions of "Sunrise on the Reaping," Haymitch and his fellow District 12 tributes, including Maysilee Donner (Mckenna Grace), align themselves not with the super-charged Career tributes from wealthy districts but other underdogs, dubbing themselves "the Newcomers." One of those Newcomers is Ampert Latier (Percy Daggs IV), the son of former District 3 victor Beetee Latier (Kelvin Harrison Jr.) who's only in the Games because the Capitol wants to punish Beetee for insubordination.

Sources indicate that ampert, Beetee, and Haymitch hatch a blueprint to smuggle an explosive into the arena and blow up a water tank that could flood the entire mechanism of the arena, and though Haymitch does set it off, the arena survives ... and the Gamemakers summarily punish him by killing Ampert with "muttations," or genetically engineered animals, in the form of squirrels. "I never even get a glimpse of Ampert, just writhing furry bodies fighting for a piece of him," Haymitch indicates in the book, and the movie does show this. It does not, however, show this:.

"Panting, I watch them fade away. Then I turn back to what I am meant to witness. A small white skeleton, stripped clean to the bone. No flesh or clothing remains, only an ax at its right side, my knife at its left. My lips move, but no sound comes out. 'Buddy?' I stumble forward, spotting his tracker, wedged just below his elbow. There is no one to comfort, to ease out of this world. Ampert's been swallowed up by the Capitol, and his coffin will hold only these pearly white bones.".

In the on-screen version, we simply see Ampert's body — not a clean skeleton.

According to recent reports, another newcomer that forms an alliance with Haymitch and Maysilee is Wellie, a diminutive District 6 tribute who's played in the film by Rada Rae. In the movie, as the tributes' numbers start to dwindle, Haymitch hears Wellie's token — a small bicycle bell — and is lured into a trap by Career tribute and formidable District 1 player Silka Sharp (Laura Marcus). The movie then skips ahead to that finale showdown between Silka and Haymitch, from which Haymitch emerges as the victor. The book is, again, far more explicit:.

"Rounding a final clump of saplings, I freeze in horror at what awaits. Silka stands like a statue, her snot-green outfit splattered in bright red. In her right hand, her ax. Her left holds Wellie's head, eyes still open, mouth agape. The only movement, the only sound, comes from the blood dripping into the pine needles on the forest floor. Wellie's body lies crumpled in a heap a few feet away. The shiny silver bicycle bell. The blowgun. The child-sized boots. The tiny knife in her bird claw. Dove-colored feathers. Headless baby chick. I could live ten thousand years and never erase this sight from my memory.".

According to recent reports, it makes complete sense that the film version of "Sunrise on the Reaping" doesn't feature a kid's decapitated head — the movie is rated PG-13, after all. Still, if you haven't read "Sunrise on the Reaping," you should (it's really good!), and you should also know that it dials up the violence ante in a major way. "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping," which is overall extremely true to the book but scales back some of its most stomach-churning moments, is in theaters now.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that apple dropped iOS 27.2.1 last week, patching a handful of security vulnerabilities and bugs—including two iMessage flaws that let people read messages they shouldn't.
  • Apple is currently beta testing the third major patch in the iOS 27 era, and anyone—developer and public tester alike—is free to install it at their leisure.
  • With the second iOS 27.3 developer beta, Apple is introducing face unlock for the iPhone Duo.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that apple dropped iOS 27.2.1 last week, patching a handful of security vulnerabilities and bugs—including two iMessage flaws that let people read messages they shouldn't. But while most of us are running this version (or should install it as soon as possible), others are running something different—iOS 27.3.

Apple is currently beta testing the third major patch in the iOS 27 era, and anyone—developer and public tester alike—is free to install it at their leisure. With it, comes the return of the Health app, vertical Safari tabs, and Siri AI app actions, among other upcoming features. But for users of Apple's first foldable, the iPhone Duo, iOS 27.3 brings two rather notable changes—both of which are for the better.

With the second iOS 27.3 developer beta, Apple is introducing face unlock for the iPhone Duo. The foldable famously ships with Touch ID, the first upcoming iPhone since the third-gen iPhone SE to do so. While that isn't a problem per se, many of us are used to unlocking our iPhones with our faces. This patch just lets new Duo owners keep up with that muscle memory.

Now, take note: This isn't Face ID. No software enhancement can introduce upcoming hardware, so the iPhone Duo still doesn't have the camera tech required to power Apple's Face ID system. As such, the Duo's face unlock is likely not as secure as Face ID on other iPhones. Perhaps that's why your iPhone Duo will require Touch ID for Apple Pay and passwords, or after 45 minutes of inactivity. This feature seems to be one of pure convenience: If you want to be able to unlock your Duo with your face (at least, some of the time), you can.

According to recent reports, what's more, this isn't a default setting. If you're running the beta, or if you're reading this after iOS 27.3 drops, you can find the option in Settings > Touch ID & Passcode.

It has been revealed that apple made a major deal about the continuity involved with opening and closing the iPhone Duo. As you do, your content moves with you seamlessly—a very Apple thing to do. That remarked, you might expect folding the Duo to lock it, but it doesn't. You need to hit the side button to actually put the phone to sleep.

Industry observers note that iOS 27.3 changes that. If you so choose, you can enable a setting to lock your Duo whenever you close it. That won't work for everyone, of course—some users may still want to move between modes without worrying about locking their Duos. But for those who would rather lock their devices whenever they fold them up, the newly introduced option is under Settings > Display & Brightness.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Peter Farrelly's "I Play Rocky" tells the story of the making of the very first "Rocky" movie. Anthony Ippolito plays "Rocky" star/writer Sylvester Stallone, and much of the film centers on his negotiations with "Rocky" producers Irwin Winkler (P.J. Byrne) and Robert Chartoff (Toby Kebbel). The movie also traces the early romantic days between Stallone and his first wife, Sasha Czack, who kept their home in order and offered support — while pregnant — throughout the production of "Rocky.".

In a recent development, sasha is played by AnnaSophia Robb, who has been racking up screen credits since she was a kid. Her first major screen role was that of the title character in the 2004 TV movie "Samantha: An American Girl Holiday," and she rapidly became one of the more ubiquitous child actors of her generation. Just a year later, she appeared in the dog-based film "Because of Winn-Dixie" and played the bratty Violet Beauregard in Tim Burton's "Charlie and the Chocolate Factory." Then, the year after that, she played a possibly evil child in "The Reaping" and starred opposite Josh Hutcherson in the heartbreaking book turned film "Bridge to Terabithia," which is easily one of the saddest movies Disney has ever made.

Robb has only continued to work steadily up to the present. She's popped up in low-profile straight-to-video movies like "Spy School," franchise starters like "Jumper," reboots like "Race to Witch Mountain," and soulful dramedies such as "The Way Way Back." Meanwhile, on the TV side of things, she's starred in the "Sex and the City" prequel show "The Carrie Diaries," PBS's "Mercy Street," and NBC's short-lived crime drama series "Grosse Pointe Garden Society." Her acting career is a healthy mix of projects massive and small, and she comes across as wholly devoted in practically all of them, "I Play Rocky" included.

Industry observers note that those who might be concerned about AnnaSophia Robb's personal well-being as a former child actor (a profession that doesn't always treat kids well) should know that she has always endeavored to live a regular life beyond her career. As she told the Arapahoe Herald in 2009:.

It has been revealed that "Living in Colorado grounds me, it makes me keep perspective. [... When I fly to Los Angeles], all my problems in Colorado disappear, and I start to think about work. I change positions. I only think about working stuff, and all of my stuff at school seems so small [and vice versa].".

This seems healthy for a teenager traversing Hollywood, and she appears to have survived high school well enough. When CBS News caught up with her in 2014, she had enrolled at Fresh York University and explained that she never wanted to be a "star," per se, noting that she's rather devoted to her craft. Indeed, Robb has apparently succeeded in showbiz by retaining a healthy personal life and remaining focused on acting rather than stardom. And her career has offered her a wide variety of roles in which to ply her craft.

Recent findings suggest that case in point: Robb is excellent in "I Play Rocky" and plays Sasha Czack as a no-nonsense individual who speaks very frankly to Sylvester Stallone. To be sure, Robb possesses a natural confidence that continues to serve her very well. "I Play Rocky" itself may be "syrupy" (to quote /Film's review of the movie), but Anthony Ippolito is a standout as Stallone, and Robb does not vanish next to him, either.

"I Play Rocky" is presently playing in theaters.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that ever since Tony premiered on the 2026 movie schedule, I’ve been looking forward to rewatching it with an HBO Max subscription. That’s because it’s such a lovely and unexpectedly heartwarming film about Anthony Bourdain’s cooking origins, and I found myself wanting to hang out in Provincetown again. However, while I did that, I also learned that the director Matt Johnson and star Dominic Sessa don’t exactly feel the same way about the film, as they described making it as “being stabbed in the stomach.”.

When CinemaBlend’s Hannah Saulic sat down to chat with the cast and director of the critically acclaimed Tony, she told them she loved the movie and described it as a “warm hug.” Matt Johnson went on to say he’s actually heard this sentiment from “so many people.” And Stavros Halkias, who plays Dimitri in the movie, noted that “it is sentimental.”.

I couldn’t agree more. The found family element of this film is honestly quite wholesome (despite the chaos). Along with that, hanging out with Tony as he figures out his life and falls in love with cooking is a really good time. Plus, there are parts of Tony that genuinely make me emotional. So, yes, in many ways, the movie is heartwarming, because he finds his people and his calling, and who wouldn’t want to spend time watching him do that?

According to recent reports, however, making this movie was a totally different story. Making that point very clear, Dominic Sessa, who plays Tony, and Johnson, who directed it, had this to say:.

Well, I can’t say I blame Sessa, specifically, for having this reaction. I mean, the best gag in Tony is the one where he gets splashed in the face with water over and over again. He told us that filming those scenes “sucked,” and Johnson described Sessa’s experience with this gag as “a kind of prison torture.".

So, I can see why they’d also note that filming the movie didn’t feel like a hug, and in a way felt like getting “stabbed in the stomach.”.

Sources indicate that however, again, that’s not how it reads on screen. As a movie, Tony is wonderful and not a torturous watch at all. To that point, Stavros Halkias jumped into the conversation to say:.

Your Daily Blend of Entertainment News.

Well, loukoumades are Greek donuts with honey, and they look delectable. And like Halkias pointed out, Tony is like a warm treat for viewers. Between Tony learning how to cook with Antonio Banderas’ Ciro, his realization that this is what he wanted to do with his life, and that Eric Ripert cameo at the end of the movie that comes with the first time Tony refers to himself as Anthony, it’s hard not to feel heartwarming energy radiating off this A24 flick.

However, when you rewatch it and feel that way, just make sure to remember and appreciate the fact that it was not that warm and cozy to make.

Latest Update: Yellowjackets Season 4 Features The Show's Most Heartbreaking Scene Yet

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Spoilers ahead for "Yellowjackets" Season 4, Episode 1, "Hivemind.".

It has been revealed that "Yellowjackets" Season 4 isn't letting up on the heartache, even now that the girls are out of the Wilderness. The show has had plenty of tearjerking moments already, from Jackie's (Ella Purnell) death in Season 1 to Shauna's (Sophie Nélisse) stillbirth in Season 2. But "Hivemind" has one to rival all of those, especially if, like me, Natalie (Sophie Thatcher) is your favorite.

Last season, Natalie snuck away from the girls' latest cannibal hunt and used a salvaged satellite phone to call for help. "Hivemind" picks up with everyone freshly rescued and recuperating in a Canadian hospital. The team's parents all fly in — including the parents who then discover that their kids didn't make it, like Mari's (Alexa Barajas) mom (Patricia De León).

The surviving Yellowjackets and their parents reunite — except for Natalie, because her mom didn't bother to show up. That everyone else's parents came only makes it worse, like the universe twisting the knife in her side yet again. She has to stand alone surrounded by reminders of the parental love she's never had and face that she's back to being the neglected kid she was before the plane crash. No wonder Natalie makes a quick exit and bums a cigarette off a hospital worker.

Sources indicate that when Natalie hears the authorities couldn't reach her mother, she smiles through the tears and states "sounds about right." You spend 19 months thinking your daughter is probably dead, and you don't drop everything when there's a chance she isn't? What kind of mother does that? We've seen before that Natalie had a rough home life. Her dad was an abusive drunk, and when Natalie threatened him with a rifle, he grabbed it and accidentally shot himself, for which Natalie's mother blames her.

According to recent reports, when we initially see Natalie in "Hivemind," she's taking her first hot shower in 19 months, as if also washing off her brutal time in the Wilderness and her sins while there. Then the rest of the episode drops cold water on her. She kept her teammates alive through the winter as a hunter and leader, and she led the effort to get them home in the last stretch of Season 3. Her reward is resettling into her crappy life.

In a recent development, on one hand, it's easy to forget struggles like a broken home when you're stuck miles away from civilization. Or, alternatively, this only makes Natalie more heroic, for she knew she didn't have much of a home to go back to but still risked everything for everyone else. But let's not overlook Natalie's (cannibalistic) complicity, either. She's the team's savior but not a saint, and that conflict is what makes her so compelling.

Back in the Season 2 episode "It Chooses," Natalie — the starving girls' chosen sacrifice — lets Javi (Luciano Leroux) drown so they can eat him instead. I asked after Season 2 if we'd been misjudging Natalie as the "good one," the same question Natalie was asking herself. Now, I'd say the answer is yes and no. She's good but not so much that she'll throw her own life away for someone else. Most people never have their morality put to the test like that, but Natalie did. She failed and has to live with proof of the kind of person she is. Now, in "Hivemind," she faces what the life she fought to hold onto so hard looks like. Before she could assuage her guilt with the imagination of rescue, now the reality can't give her that same solace.

When Natalie goes for the smoke, the hospital worker states she shouldn't be smoking. "I shouldn't be alive," Natalie replies. Is she talking about the realistic odds of surviving 19 months stranded? Of trading her life for Javi's? Of deserving to be alive? All of the above? Searching for comfort with a cigarette ties together well with Natalie in the adult timeline (Juliette Lewis), who had developed a drug addiction to cope with her guilt.

Natalie also stated in the pilot, during a rehab group session, that she lost her purpose after the Wilderness. Now we know that she had blossomed into a leader out there. It's important to contrast her with the group's other queens, Shauna and Lottie, because all three became people they couldn't be back home.

Lottie, without access to her medication, embraced her illness as clairvoyance and became a prophet. Shauna lived in Jackie's shadow her whole life, then came into her own in the most horrifying way possible. Before the plane crash, Natalie was viewed by everyone as a burnout. She was already hitting drugs and liquor in high school, and her teammates looked down on her for that, for her sexual proclivity, and for being poorer than them. In the Wilderness, she became a leader without intending to become one.

Industry observers note that in "Hivemind," Lottie is almost catatonic, and Shauna is stewing in silent anger. None of the three Antler Queens are going to have an easy time readjusting, but with Natalie, it feels like she could have if she'd had a better support system waiting for her. Natalie's mom not showing up for her may lack the violence of other "Yellowjackets" tearjerker moments, but it remains quietly heartbreaking all the same.

"Yellowjackets" is streaming on Paramount+.

Breaking: 10 Books Like ‘Dungeon Crawler Carl’ You Should Read Next

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There’s nothing quite like Dungeon Crawler Carl, Matt Dinniman’s hilarious, inventive, and surprisingly emotional book series about a man in his underwear forced to fight his way through a livestreamed game show based on dungeon-crawling video games that takes place after an alien takeover of Earth. (Did I mention he's accompanied by his ex-girlfriend’s suddenly talkative cat?).

The premise should not work, but it sure does—and it makes more sense if you know it fits into a popular genre known as "LitRPG," a blend of "literature" and "role-playing game." If you've torn through all eight books released so far and you're looking for more reads that blend surprisingly deep hilarity with tabletop and video game rules (or just similar feels), here are 10 books you should check out.

Sources indicate that an isekai story that lands in the sweet spot for DCC fans, He Who Fights with Monsters kicks off with Jason—a completely normal, kind of boring middle manager—waking up in a strange hedge maze, completely nude (even his hair is gone). He has magic that works like a video game, and has to deal with quests that slowly give him clothes (it’s a relief when he finally acquires some pants), force him to survive cannibals, and hunt down various monsters that definitely need killing. It’s got the same “gaming rules” structure as DCC and a similarly absurdist tone, with just the right spice of darkness.

It has been revealed that the Cradle series by Will Wight isn’t a LitRPG, and it doesn’t have Carl’s focus on humor, but it’s another progression fantasy with enough game-like elements to be a great match. Lindon is an “unsouled,” incapable of gaining any of the sacred arts and doomed to a life without a future. His lack of power makes Lindon ferociously determined to find an alternative path to power and success, and that’s what drives this story. He has to find creative ways to move forward, and slowly this leads him to a path that just might make him the most powerful person in his world. DCC fans will love the progression and the tone.

Industry observers note that one of the key elements of any video game is the respawn—you get killed, but you pop back up to try again, sometimes at the beginning, sometimes at a save point. Django Wexler leverages that mechanic to great effect in How to Become the Dark Lord and Die Trying. Davi has been summoned to a fantasy world to be the hero, the person who defeats the Dark Lord and saves the day—but she’s failed (and died) so many times, she’s fed up, and decides that on this run through, she’s going to switch sides and become the Dark Lord, using all her knowledge gained from endless replays to her advantage. The humor is pitch-black the way DCC fans like it, and the progressive structure is a perfect fit.

Sources indicate that is Princess Donut your favorite part of Dungeon Crawler Carl? Of course she is. In that case, check out Andrew Seiple’s Threadbare series. Threadbare is a stuffed bear brought to magical life in a failed experiment. He’s a foot tall, full of stuffing, and extremely dumb when the story begins. But when he’s rescued by a little girl and plunged into a horrible series of dangers, Threadbare has to find a way to level up. Like DCC, Threadbare starts off leaning into the absurdity and humor, then slowly gains emotional gravitas as the story progresses.

If you play tabletop RPGs, you’ve encountered a Murderhobo or two: A character who solves all their problems by killing—even members of their own party. Luke doesn’t aspire to be a Murderhobo—he just wants to take over the family business and hang with his buddies. But when an invasion threatens the kingdom, everyone over the age of 17 is ordered to be tested for Potential. Luke’s friends all test high and join the Ascender Corps, traveling to different planes for training. Luke tests ... very low, and when he steps through a portal to engage in his training, he finds himself without any guidance or training in a strange, deadly world where his only chance of survival is to murder his way through it. It’s dark, darkly funny, and a progression fantasy like no other.

If you’re looking for a book series that combines the dark, chaotic humor, absurd game mechanics, and surprising emotional depth of Carl, here’s Ryan “Quicksave” Romano, a man who has the unique ability to literally create a save point in his existence that allows him to go back and redo things whenever he dies. Searching for a childhood friend, he becomes embroiled in a violent gang war that lets him make good use of his power—but underneath the snark and the insanity of Ryan’s existence is a surprisingly affecting story of a man who has suffered, and suffered countless tragedies that are definitely taking their toll.

If your fave bit of DCC is Carl himself—a mediocre dude in an extraordinary situation—you should read Dennis E. Taylor’s fantastic Bobiverse books. Bob is a software engineer who hits it major and promptly dies, waking up to discover a century has passed and he’s been repurposed as an AI controlling a space probe searching for new planets for humanity to inhabit. If he fails in his mission (and he’s not the only probe out there), he’ll be turned off for good. Luckily, he can make copies of himself, and he’s pretty smart. The humor here is smart and soaked in pop culture, making it a perfect match for DCC fans.

In a recent development, want more of Carl’s absurdist humor? Mayor of Noobtown is the LitRPG you’re looking for. Jim dies and wakes up in a video game-esque universe and finds himself stuck in the zone designated for newbies—players with no experience, skill, or hope. The area fell out of the mainline progression mechanic a long time ago, so there doesn’t seem to be a way to gain power, and the monsters are not at all concerned about the unfairness of it all, so Jim has to figure out how to advance in a universe that seems designed to kill him (again).

According to recent reports, if you want to lean into the meta side of things, check out Scathing Reviewer, written by an author who goes by the unusual pen name "BananaDragon." Liu Peijin is the author of a sprawling LitRPG web novel, and she’s used to the bad reviews and complaints from readers—and quite combative about it. When her books’ universe blossoms into a very dangerous new reality, she should be perfectly positioned to survive, having written the story in the first place. But her story becoming real also means her insufferable protagonist is real, and all those nasty critics are now passing judgment on her entire existence. It’s a dark, funny takedown of the entire genre itself, and DCC fans will love it.

If you want a story that parallels the dungeon crawling aspect of DCC, Andrew Rowe’s Arcane Ascension series is the ticket. The Serpent Spire is a tower of constantly changing traps, puzzles, and dangerous creatures. If you enter and survive, you emerge with magical powers. Corin Cadence’s brother entered the Serpent Spire years ago and never returned—and now Corin is determined not only to survive, but to make it to the top, where legend claims a goddess will grant you whatever you wish. And what Corin wants is his brother back. It’s a literal progression combined with LitRPG rules, game-inspired puzzle-solving, and a complex magic system that fans of Carl will definitely enjoy.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The world of Baldur’s Gate 3 is expanding beyond video games once again, with a new official prequel novel set to explore the darker corners of the Forgotten Realms. The upcoming book will take readers beneath the streets of Baldur’s Gate, where a murder threatens to expose the secrets of a secretive religious order.

It has been revealed that titled Baldur’s Gate 3: Shadowheart, the upcoming fantasy novel comes from Tasha Suri, the World Fantasy Award-winning author of the Burning Kingdoms trilogy. It is scheduled to arrive on June 8, 2027, and is available to preorder now at major retailers.

As the title suggests, the story centers on Shadowheart, the cleric of Shar who became one of the most popular companions in Larian Studios' hit RPG.

According to the official book description, Shadowheart is a devoted follower of the goddess of darkness and loss. Living beneath Baldur’s Gate in a secretive underground church, she has embraced the belief that sacrificing memories is the key to gaining strength.

However, when a member of her religious order is murdered in the city's wealthy Upper City, Shadowheart is tasked with investigating alongside several fellow acolytes. Among them are an ambitious Griefguard named Mirie, a cynical propagandist named Caldan, and Nocturne, a charming quartermaster whose intentions Shadowheart has reason to question.The investigation soon reveals that Baldur’s Gate's wealthiest district has plenty of secrets of its own. As Shadowheart encounters unfamiliar temptations and begins questioning the comforts of her faith, she must solve the murder before her devotion is called into question.

The novel offers another opportunity to explore the backstories and world of Baldur’s Gate 3 beyond the game itself. While the book's description doesn't reveal exactly how its events connect to the RPG's broader timeline, its focus on Shadowheart's life within Shar's church should give fans a closer look at the character's history.

Industry observers note that the Shadowheart novel is the latest expansion of the Baldur’s Gate 3 universe beyond video games. Astarion, another fan-favorite companion, has already received his own prequel novel written by T. Kingfisher, alongside other character-focused stories and comics. The franchise is also heading to television, with HBO developing an official Baldur’s Gate series from The Last of Us co-creator Craig Mazin. Unlike the upcoming Shadowheart novel, the show is expected to pick up after the events of Baldur’s Gate 3.

Baldur’s Gate 3: Shadowheart launches June 8, 2027.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Imagine taking the exploration and secrets of The Legend of Zelda, blending in the branching quests and consequential decisions of Baldur’s Gate 3, and dropping the whole thing onto a cursed pirate island. Sounds like an unusual combination, but one indie RPG brings these elements together, with dangerous creatures, challenging boss fights and multiple endings. Better yet, PC players can claim it for free for a limited time.

According to recent reports, mark of the Deep, developed by Mad Mimic and released in January 2025, is now available on the Epic Games Store for free. The game follows Marcus “Rookie” Ramsey, whose ship is wrecked on an island that most people know only through rumors. With the rest of his crew, the Angry Mermaids, missing, Rookie must explore the island and uncover the mystery behind its curse, which is tied to its native inhabitants, known as the Old Folks.

You see Zelda here once you look closely at how the island unfolds. Mark of the Deep uses an isometric, top-down view and encourages players to explore its connected areas. Rookie gradually gains upcoming abilities that change how he moves through the world and handles enemies. Some routes stay out of reach until he has the right skill, giving players a reason to return to explored places. There are also secrets and side quests to find along the way.

Sources indicate that this isn’t a party-based, turn-based RPG, though, so the Baldur’s Gate comparison isn’t about the genre. Mark of the Deep is a single-player action adventure, and its fights take more from the Soulslike genre. Its role-playing side comes through in the people Rookie meets, the quests he can take on and the decisions he makes. The game lets players help characters affected by the island’s corruption, and those choices can influence how the story ends.

Recent findings suggest that for the crucial part of combat, the developers list more than 80 enemies and 16 bosses, including abyssal creatures, undead enemies and cultists. Rookie can unlock newly introduced skills, weapons and trinkets as he progresses, allowing him to improve his fighting options. Boss encounters can be challenging, requiring players to learn enemy attack patterns and adjust their approach.

It has been revealed that the island also has plenty to explore, although the lack of an in-game map can make navigation frustrating at times. Its atmosphere and exploration are appealing, but players should be prepared to spend some time figuring out where to go next.

There’s a time limit on the giveaway, but not on playing the game once it has been claimed. Search for Mark of the Deep on the Epic Games Store and add it to your library before the offer ends on November 26 at 4 p.m. UTC. You don’t need to download and install the game to claim it for free; just add it and a copy becomes yours forever.

Mark of the Deep is also a fairly modest download by current PC standards: you don’t need a powerful rig to play this Zelda-inspired pirate adventure. For your reference, Epic lists a 5GB storage requirement, 4GB RAM and a dual-core 2.4GHz processor as the minimum specifications.

It has been revealed that the Legend of Zelda franchise follows the adventures of Link, an elf-like Hylian, and Princess Zelda as they protect the land of Hyrule from the evil warlord-turned-demon king Ganon. The series is known for its mix of action, adventure, and puzzle-solving elements, often revolving around the collection of the Triforce, a powerful relic left by the goddesses who created Hyrule.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Don't read any poems about ravens if you haven't seen "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping." Spoilers ahead!

According to recent reports, we don't know precisely when the Hunger Games world exists. We just know, from the books and films, that North America has been redrawn into a totalitarian regime called Panem by that point in the future. There's a very interesting reference to American culture, though, in both the novel and movie version of "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping," the origin story of future District 12 mentor and rebel Haymitch Abernathy (Joseph Zada in this film). Specifically, Edgar Allan Poe's poem "The Raven" just ... exists.

Sources indicate that the book takes great pains to "transform" this poem — which begins with the line "Once upon a midnight dreary, while I pondered, weak and weary" — into a song, which gives Haymitch's girlfriend Lenore Dove Baird (Whitney Peak) her first name. As Haymitch indicates of Lenore Dove, a member of District 12's musical Covey, "She tends to take a dark view of things, but maybe that's to be expected from someone named for a dead girl. Well, half for the dead girl called Lenore in this old poem and half for a shade of gray, which I found out the day I met her.".

In case you're foggy on "The Raven," here's a snippet:.

Industry observers note that ah, distinctly I remember it was in the bleak December; And each separate dying ember wrought its ghost upon the floor. Eagerly I wished the morrow;—vainly I had sought to borrow From my books surcease of sorrow—sorrow for the lost Lenore— For the rare and radiant maiden whom the angels name Lenore— Nameless here for evermore.

Sources indicate that interestingly, the "Sunrise on the Reaping" book by Suzanne Collins never mentions Poe by name. The movie, however, takes a different approach.

Again, in Suzanne Collins' 2025 novel "Sunrise on the Reaping," the author makes it clear that "The Raven" is a song of, I suppose, unknown provenance. As Haymitch explains while he's preparing for the Games, he keeps dreaming about Lenore and thinking about what he calls her "name song," saying, "In it, a guy loses the love of his life, Lenore, and he's going crazy for missing her. Then this big old raven highlights up at his house and won't leave and whenever he asks the bird anything, it just indicates 'Nevermore' — which, as you can imagine, just makes him crazier.".

Across the board, "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping" is a pretty faithful adaptation of the novel, and a scene between Haymitch and Capitol cameraman Plutarch Heavensbee (Jesse Plemons on-screen) plays out roughly the same as it does on the page. There is one notable difference, though, which is that the film has a physical prop book that indicates "'The Raven' by Edgar Allan Poe" on the cover.

Both versions have Plutarch ask Haymitch if he knows what "nepenthe," a mythical potion, means when the Hunger Games tribute sees a bottle of it on a bar. When Plutarch inquires if Haymitch has heard of it in the book, he internally scoffs: "Not only have I heard of it, I know it from the poem that gave my love her name. I'm tired of being patronized, so I decide to put him in his place." When Haymitch recites a line about nepenthe from the poem, Plutarch finishes it in both versions. So, why is this poem so horrifyingly perfect for this Hunger Games story?

Industry observers note that putting aside the wild idea of Edgar Allan Poe being, I think, the only tangible link between our world and Panem, Suzanne Collins picked a horribly appropriate name for Lenore Dove Baird. The woman in "The Raven" is, obviously, dead, and by the end of "Sunrise on the Reaping," Lenore Dove meets the same fate.

In a recent development, when Haymitch, working with fellow tribute Ampert Latier (Percy Daggs IV) and Ampert's father, Haymitch's assigned mentor, and former District 3 victor Beetee (Kelvin Harrison Jr.), tries to destroy the Games arena itself by blowing up a subterranean water tank, he does technically succeed. Unfortunately, the water tank bursts, yet the arena remains intact, and Haymitch wins the Games by utilizing a force field just outside of the arena's range ... and is summarily punished when he returns home to District 12. Not only does he find his house burning to ash immediately upon arrival, he learns that his mother and younger brother, his only family members, are inside. Then, not long after, he reunites with Lenore and feeds her a gumdrop, her favorite candy ... but it's a poisoned bag direct from President Snow, and she dies, too.

Sources indicate that "The raven. The unforgiving songbird. Repeatedly reminding me of President Snow's crystal-clear message to me on my homecoming," Haymitch thinks to himself bitterly as he mourns. "That I will never get to love anyone ever again. Nevermore. Because he will make sure they end up dying a horrible death." Still, the word "Nevermore" ends the film adaptation as Haymitch surveys the now-peaceful reaping site, giving it a slightly brighter meaning when the story ends on-screen.

"The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping" is in theaters now.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There are a lot of characters in the wider "Hunger Games" universe, so I'll forgive you if you're only familiar with some of the bigger players like Katniss Everdeen (Jennifer Lawrence), Haymitch Abernathy (Joseph Zada in his origin film and Woody Harrelson in the original movies), Coriolanus Snow (Tom Blyth, Ralph Fiennes, and Donald Sutherland at various points throughout his life), Peeta Mellark (Josh Hutcherson), or Lucy Gray Baird (Rachel Zegler). The latest installment in the literary and cinematic franchise, "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping," brings back some familiar faces and introduces newly introduced ones too — so, who, exactly, is Proserpina Trinket?

According to recent reports, introduced in both the book and film version of "Sunrise on the Reaping," Proserpina Trinket is a bubbly, enthusiastic, and quick-thinking young stylist working to prepare Hunger Games tributes for all the Capitol-centric pomp and circumstance that takes place before the bloody Games themselves. (Yes, the teenage tributes get all dolled up before they're forced to fight to the death in a dangerous arena that's also trying to kill them. This world is sick!).

We don't know a ton about Prosperina besides the fact that she works with the extremely unreliable Magno Stift (Billy Porter), she's assigned to work on Zada's Haymitch alongside Vitus (Edvin Ryding), and her older sister is future District 12 chaperone and stylist Effie Trinket (played in this film by Elle Fanning and the original movies by Elizabeth Banks). What we definitely know is that she's played by Iris Apatow, a rising talent from a famous family who's shown up in a handful of TV highlights and several huge comedy movies from the 2000s.

Iris Apatow was born in 2002, and odds are you're familiar with her family. Her older sister, Maude Apatow, starred in "Euphoria" throughout its entire run. Her mother, Leslie Mann, is an acclaimed comedic actor. Then there's her dad Judd Apatow, a comedy kingmaker, producer, writer, and director who's helped make projects like "Superbad" and "Bridesmaids" and directed his own like "The 40-Year-Old Virgin," "Knocked Up," "Funny People," and "This is 40." Let's talk about those last three, because all of them feature the youngest Apatow. (The less mentioned about Judd Apatow's 2022 COVID movie "The Bubble," the better.).

Sources indicate that maude and Iris Apatow play Sadie and Charlotte, respectively, in both "Knocked Up" and "This is 40" — with their on-screen mother, Debbie, portrayed by Mann, and their father Pete by Paul Rudd as an Apatow stand-in. As for "Funny People," they also play Mann's daughters (in this one, Maude is Mable and Iris is Ingrid) with Mann as Laura, the ex-girlfriend of comedian and actor George Simmons (Adam Sandler), who's dealing with a life-changing health crisis. Sure, the Apatow daughters don't do a ton here, but they flesh out the universe in all three of their dad's films ... and it's notable that we watched Maude and Iris grow up on-screen, basically.

All things considered, Iris Apatow's career is just getting started. Still, over the past few years, she's dabbled in more adult fare (especially on the small screen), so it definitely seems like she's trying to show off her range.

Sources indicate that from 2016 to 2018, Apatow portrayed a supporting character, Arya Hopkins, who's tutored by series lead Gus (Paul Rust) on the Netflix TV show "Love," while on another Netflix exclusive, "Unstable," she appeared alongside Rob Lowe and his real-life son John Owen Love. The latter duo play tech CEO Ellis Dragon and his creatively inclined son Jackson, respectively, whereas Apatow plays Anna, an intern at Ellis' manufacturer, itself aptly named Dragon, who also happens to be the former stepdaughter of the company's CFO Anna ("Fleabag" standout Sian Clifford).

According to recent reports, then there's "Tell Me Lies." A deliciously dramatic and dishy Hulu series created by Meaghan Oppenheimer, "Tell Me Lies" adapts (and improves) the book of the same name by Carola Lovering and ran for three seasons on Hulu. Apatow shows up as a college student named Amanda in the third and final season, creating a problem for series regular Bree (Cat Missal) as she mentally and emotionally recovers from an affair with a professor named Oliver (Tom Ellis). After she finally gets out of Oliver's clutches, Bree notices that Amanda seems to be Oliver's next victim, sending her into a spiral.

You can see Apatow as Proserpina in "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping" in theaters now.

No. If you find the product you're looking for with a major discount right now, get it. It's not likely to drop any lower, but it could always run out of stock. Take advantage of price matching or guarantees instead of waiting. Remember, you can always return products later if you change your mind. For the majority of products, the deal from Black Friday will be the same one on Cyber Monday.

Latest Update: Hexed Might Be A Major Misfire For Disney Animation At The Box Office

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that disney has produced many of the best animated movies of all time.
  • Sources indicate that "Hexed" is currently eyeing an opening in the $23 million range, per Box Office Theory.
  • Sources indicate that more than A24's "Club Kid" or or the "Hershey" biopic, also releasing over Thanksgiving, it's "The Hunger Games" that will be a bigger issue for Disney's latest.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that disney has produced many of the best animated movies of all time. They've been doing it longer than anyone else and, arguably, better than anyone else for decades. Unfortunately though, original animation has been a tough sell to audiences in recent years, and Disney's "Hexed" looks like it's going to suffer at the box office as a result of this trend.

Sources indicate that "Hexed" is currently eyeing an opening in the $23 million range, per Box Office Theory. That's across the full five-day, Wednesday to Sunday stretch since this movie is opening mid-week for the Thanksgiving holiday. The comedy "Focker In-Law" pits Ben Stiller against Ariana Grande and looks to win the weekend with around $36 million. For what it's worth, earlier tracking (via Deadline) had both movies doing between $40 and $50 million across the five-day stretch.

Sources indicate that more than A24's "Club Kid" or or the "Hershey" biopic, also releasing over Thanksgiving, it's "The Hunger Games" that will be a bigger issue for Disney's latest. "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping" will be a bigger hit than you realize, doing well over $100 million on opening weekend. That means, in its second frame, it could still easily take number one over Thanksgiving.

According to recent reports, disney's latest centers on an impulsive and unconventional teenage girl named Billie (Hailee Steinfeld) who discovers secret magical abilities which. Once unleashed, they hurtle her out of suburbia and into a vast witch realm called Hexe. Fawn Veerasunthorn and Jason Hand directed the movie, with Josie Trinidad co-directing.

The massive concern for "Hexed" is that these movies don't come cheap. We're looking at a budget of at least $150 million, if not much more. Even at $150 million, an opening under $30 million across a robust, long holiday weekend is close to a death sentence. Yes, there are overseas markets to account for and family-friendly movies can have long legs. Even so, the early estimates are rough, to put it kindly.

It's especially disappointing because this feels like the right place on the calendar for the movie. "Moana 2" smashed box office records and led to the biggest Thanksgiving ever in 2024. That eventually became a $1 billion hit for Disney. But that was a sequel to a much-beloved move from the 2010s. Originals, from both Disney Animation and Pixar, have struggled mightily in the 2020s.

Case in point, "Strange World" bombed at the box office in 2022, taking in just $73 million worldwide. "Hexed" doesn't appear to be in such terrible shape but it's not looking good. Disney's "Wish" was also a significant disappointment at the box office in 2023, doing $255 million worldwide. Decent for an original movie by today's standards but not nearly good enough to turn a profit.

Industry observers note that the only thing Disney can hope for is that word of mouth amongst moviegoers is outstanding, which could give "Hexed" unusually long legs. Or that tracking is just wildly off and the movie actually comes in closer to earlier estimates. Either way, as it stands, this one looks like it just has one too many hurdles to clear.

Disney's "Hexed" hits theaters on November 25, 2026.

All 14 Witches In Agatha All Along Explained
