📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It’s been quite a year for Curry Barker. In September 2025, he brought his $700,000 horror film to the Toronto International Film Festival, where it sparked a bidding war that Focus Features won for $17 million. That hefty price tag turned into the deal of the century, as “Obsession” went on to become a half-billion-dollar box-office sensation, with audiences growing week to week. It was clear the then 26-year-old “YouTuber” (a moniker Barker rightfully dismisses) was something special. This was not just a flash in the pan, but a real talent with a seemingly boundless number of ideas and movies he wanted to make. His next film, “Anything but Ghosts,” was already in the can by the “Obsession” premiere, a yet-to-be-unveiled third film is in the works, while potential franchises (“Texas Chainsaw Massacre” and “Obsession,” Barker sees the One Wish Willow story device having “Knives Out” anthology-like potential) linger in the background. Related Stories Director Brian Duffield Had to Find a New Form of Visual Storytelling for ‘Whalefall’ How ‘Paper Tiger’ Evolved When Jeremy Strong and Anne Hathaway Couldn’t Reprise Their ‘Armageddon Time’ Roles.

Which is why it’s interesting that Hollywood’s hottest new director took time out from editing (he’s cutting “Ghosts” himself) and writing (“I have my next thing that I’m working on — I’m really excited about it, and nobody knows anything about it, which is super exciting”), and an unexpected Oscar campaign (“Obsession” is a legit contender for Best Picture, Actress, and Original Screenplay nominations), to make a 5-minute short film, “Mama Bear.” On this week’s episode of the Filmmaker Toolkit Podcast, Barker talked about how the success of “Obsession” interrupted his established flow of churning out short-form content for his popular YouTube channel.

According to recent reports, “I have two or three short films where I’m like, ‘Oh man, this all took off really promptly, and I have this short film idea I’ve been dying to do,” stated Barker on Toolkit. “I actually have no time to do those short films, and then justifying if it be would be worth my time to do them when I need to be writing this, I need to be editing this, and I need to be doing press for this.”.

It’s less about Barker’s desire to scratch the itch of the shorts he never got to make, but more about a hesitancy to step away completely from the iterative process by which he learned his craft — justifying the brief time he took off to make “Mama Bear” because he felt the need to sketch.

Recent findings suggest that “It’s fun to have that playground because the features are bigger stakes,” remarked Barker. “We were like, ‘Okay, this is a short film: We can do weird stuff. Let’s come up with crazy rules that don’t make sense, and experiment.’”.

Barker and his “Mama Bear” cinematographer — his young brother Riley, who worked on the “Obsession” camera department — created different rules for the camera, as Curry is still trying to hone his discipline for storytelling within longer takes. Not only would they shoot a narrow 4:3 aspect ratio, but the Barker brothers denied themselves the ability to move the camera left, right, up, down, or dolly in.

“I do have a lot to learn,” said Barker of making “Mama Bear.” “It’s so funny because I was having dinner and I told someone, ‘Oh, I’d love to shadow on Ari Aster’s set.’ And someone was like, ‘Well, you’re Curry Barker, what are you going to shadow for?’”.

His 2026 meteoric rise has allowed Barker to collect a group of more experienced peers he views as mentors — including Aster, Bill Hader, Zach Cregger, and Rian Johnson — and successful producers, like Jason Blum, investing in his career, but he believes there’s a misconception of what comes along with “making it.”.

In a recent development, “People think that once you’re in this club, you’re in the club, and everyone talks to everyone. But no — you’re in a bubble, and I want to know how Zach Cregger writes his outline. I want to watch him do it,” mentioned Barker. “You’re all alone. Your process is your own, and you figure this stuff out on your own. Once you get into this league, there’s no one telling you, ‘Well, actually you do it like this, this, and this.’ It’s whatever you learned all along your journey; that’s your process.”.

According to recent reports, one of the most impressive things about the self-taught Barker’s journey is how promptly he turned himself into a successful actor/writer/director/editor. In 2018, when Barker left Alabama to come to Los Angeles to pursue a career in movies, he saw himself as an actor. Despite all the story scenarios dancing around his head, the idea that he would become a screenwriter was laughable.

It has been revealed that “I never would’ve thought I was a screenwriter. I didn’t make great grades. I made Cs and Ds, and I wasn’t the best in English class,” said Barker, who naively assumed professional writers were the kids who won spelling bees: “I just thought to be respected as a writer you have to be that.” Barker credits taking screenwriter Aaron Sorkin’s MasterClass as what opened his eyes. “It was the first time I thought, ‘I can do this, too.’ It’s really just about being creative and cracking a story, and there are rules, there’s structure.”.

Directing organically grew out of Barker pulling together collaborators to shoot sketches and shorts for him to act in. Barker, half-joking, likes to say he realized one day that what he was doing was directing, and that he both enjoyed “telling people what to do” and had a knack for it.

Sources indicate that what Barker accomplishes in a single shot — establishing a tonal balance that teeters between horror and comedy, combining blocking and camera movement to edit within the frame — is remarkably sophisticated. But Barker, who studies and strives for what masters like Kiyoshi Kurosawa can accomplish, quickly claims he fell short in “Obsession.”.

It has been revealed that “Things that you might think we pulled off [with longer takes in ‘Obsession’], we reshot,” said Barker, who on the podcast described in detail a key early scene between Bear (Michael Johnston) and Nikki (Inde Navarrette) in the bedroom that had to be reshot because the action took too long to unfold. “I think Ari [Aster] said once that if you realize you needed to give this information in four seconds, but then it took 25 seconds, you’re stuck with 25 seconds.”.

Curry Barker, the editor, is Curry Barker, the director’s harshest critic, giving him a bird’s-eye view of what he believes is the director’s inability to envision the required pacing of how a scene will play on screen, even if it might feel unnaturally fast on set.

Recent findings suggest that “Every single oner that I’ve shot in my career has been a problem in the edit,” mentioned Barker. “I think there’s two ways to fail at something. You can either fail, realize that it didn’t work, get scared of it, and then be like, ‘Well, in my last film I did a bunch of oners and then it killed me in the edit, so I’m not going to do that anymore.’ Or you can fail, realize how you did it wrong, and try to get better at that for the next time.”.

As Barker discussed at the Future of Filmmaking Summit last month, that iterative process is key to how he got where he is, and it’s a mindset he clearly hasn’t given up. When asked how “Obsession” would have been different if he had more money, Barker doesn’t talk about locations, sets, special or visual effects, or scenes he envisioned that he couldn’t pull off — in terms of scale, he likes both writing and directing within set limitations.

“I would’ve reshot everything,” Barker answered without hesitation. “If I was finishing the edit before we got into TIFF, and you were like, ‘Dude, this is really good, we really love this movie, we think it has potential, but we want to give you $10 million to reshoot the whole thing, I would be like, ‘Deal.’ I would take it.”.

“I think it’s so funny to look back and think about that now,” Barker catches himself, knowing he’s talking about a film that broke the box office and catapulted his career. “Now I wouldn’t change anything because I would be too scared to touch it.”.

25 Best Enemies To Lovers Manhwa Ever

📅 28 Apr 2024 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1909 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Screenrant

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, romance manhwa comes in many forms, but some of the most memorable love stories begin with two people who would rather have nothing to do with each other.
  • Recent findings suggest that the enemies-to-lovers trope is especially popular in fantasy and otome isekai manhwa, where political intrigue, second chances, arranged marriages, and complicated family histories provide plenty of opportunities for romantic conflict.
  • Industry observers note that beastly Things has a distinct Twilight vibe, introducing readers to a secret society of werewolves.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, romance manhwa comes in many forms, but some of the most memorable love stories begin with two people who would rather have nothing to do with each other. Whether their animosity stems from conflicting ambitions, family rivalries, painful misunderstandings, or circumstances that force them into an uncomfortable partnership, these stories thrive on the tension between their protagonists. Watching two characters gradually abandon their resentment and discover an unexpected connection is one of the most satisfying aspects of the enemies-to-lovers genre.

Recent findings suggest that the enemies-to-lovers trope is especially popular in fantasy and otome isekai manhwa, where political intrigue, second chances, arranged marriages, and complicated family histories provide plenty of opportunities for romantic conflict. However, the trope isn't limited to historical settings or villainess reincarnation stories. From dangerous games of manipulation to hilarious workplace rivalries and relationships built on long-standing grudges, there's something for every romance fan. For readers who enjoy watching hostility gradually turn into affection, these manhwa are well worth adding to their reading lists.

Industry observers note that beastly Things has a distinct Twilight vibe, introducing readers to a secret society of werewolves. The story follows Ji-u Han, the pack leader's daughter, who harbors an inferiority complex and resents her father for not choosing her as his successor. The plot kicks off when she meets the actor Yuseung Cheo, who's actually a werewolf hunter seeking to exact revenge on the race that killed his parents. However, Ji-u also intends to use him to secure the power she so deeply craves.

Recent findings suggest that featuring a series of human murders in addition to the conflict between werewolves and hunters, the webtoon's true appeal lies in its two manipulative protagonists on opposing sides, secretly playing games with one another while inevitably beginning to develop feelings. While it features all the hallmarks of toxic relationships, such as obsession, betrayal, and hidden agendas, Beastly Things proves to be an addictive guilty pleasure that's hard to put down.

According to recent reports, the Crown Princess Scandal is a different kind of enemies-to-lovers story, as it sets aside the angst and drama in favor of absurd interactions and protagonists whose only reason for hating each other is their clashing personalities. The webtoon begins with Hwa-Yeong, who reluctantly takes her sister's place in a selection process to become the crown princess.

It has been revealed that hwa-Yeong just wants to go home, and the crown prince finds satisfaction in not letting her get away with her intends, with the plot delivering all sorts of hilarious bickering between the two. Although it feels more like a simple comedy at first, the humor doesn't overshadow the romance, and even Hwa-Yeong’s antics serve as a catalyst for the characters' emotional growth. The palpable tension between the protagonists and the way their relationship develops make The Crown Princess Scandal an especially cute and lighthearted love story.

The Hand That Once Fed offers a particularly messy interpretation of enemies-to-lovers romance, exploring what happens when a former relationship deteriorates into resentment and a desire for revenge. The story follows Evelyn Winter, a widowed duchess whose seemingly comfortable life is disrupted when Colonel Gilath Black suddenly returns. Once her devoted servant and lover, Gilath now approaches her with accusations of treason and an entirely different attitude toward the woman he once adored.

What makes this relationship particularly compelling is the dramatic reversal of their former positions. Gilath, who was once loyal to Evelyn, has become a dangerous presence in her household, while Evelyn must fight to protect her position and navigate the consequences of their shared history. Neither character is particularly straightforward, and their interactions leave readers questioning whether Gilath wants to rekindle their relationship or destroy the woman who once held his heart. With its exploration of betrayal, obsession, and unresolved feelings, The Hand That Once Fed is an excellent choice for readers who prefer their romances with plenty of psychological tension.

Sources indicate that betrayal of Dignity is a dark historical romance that puts its protagonists in a complicated relationship defined by manipulation, desperation, and conflicting interests. The story follows Chloe Verdier, a young noblewoman struggling to prevent her family from falling into ruin. When her sister Alice disappears with a mysterious man, Chloe finds herself turning to Duke Damien Thisse, a notoriously arrogant and ruthless military hero. His proposal offers a potential solution to her family's problems, but accepting his help means entering a dangerous arrangement with a man she can hardly trust.

Recent findings suggest that unlike lighter enemies-to-lovers stories, Betrayal of Dignity doesn't shy away from the uncomfortable aspects of its central relationship. Damien's controlling personality and Chloe's determination to protect herself create an ongoing struggle for power, with neither protagonist willing to surrender easily. Chloe is particularly interesting because she isn't simply swept away by the Duke's wealth or appearance; she has her own priorities and must constantly consider the consequences of her decisions. The result is an emotionally complicated romance filled with questionable choices, courtly intrigue, and a relationship that is anything but straightforward.

According to recent reports, frozen Hearts introduces a supernatural variation of the enemies-to-lovers trope, placing its protagonists on opposite sides of a dangerous conflict. The story follows Seolha, a Snow Maiden demon who has concealed her true identity while living among humans. Her carefully maintained disguise becomes increasingly difficult to protect when she attracts the attention of the Northern Prince, a man infamous for hunting and killing demons. Their circumstances eventually lead to Seolha becoming his bride, creating an unusual marriage between two individuals who should naturally be enemies.

The main appeal of Frozen Hearts comes from the secrets and conflicting loyalties surrounding its protagonists. Seolha must conceal her identity while navigating married life with someone whose reputation makes him particularly dangerous to her kind. Meanwhile, the prince must contend with a relationship that challenges the rigid beliefs underlying his demon-hunting activities. Their situation creates plenty of opportunities for suspicion, emotional conflict, and gradual character development. With its winter-inspired fantasy setting and supernatural premise, Frozen Hearts is an especially appealing choice for readers who enjoy watching characters from opposing worlds develop feelings for each other.

Dear Nemesis offers a very entertaining take on the enemies-to-lovers trope, combining reincarnation, aristocratic politics, and a romance built on a complicated history. The story follows Calmia Phlox, who receives a second chance at life after a previous existence that left her determined to reclaim her family's position and secure her future as Countess Phlox. However, her ambitions become complicated when she must compete with her beloved twin brother while navigating the schemes of those around her. Matters become even more interesting when Rudbeckia Matari, her former archenemy, unexpectedly proposes marriage.

Rather than immediately abandoning their differences, Calmia and Rudbeckia approach their engagement as a calculated arrangement, with both having their own ambitions and reasons for accepting the partnership. Their shared history makes it difficult for either to place complete trust in the other, but their political alliance gradually develops into something much more personal. With two intelligent, ambitious protagonists constantly trying to stay one step ahead of each other, Dear Nemesis delivers an especially satisfying slow-burn romance. Its combination of strategic maneuvering, family drama, and gradually developing affection makes it an excellent choice for readers who enjoy seeing former rivals become unexpected romantic partners.

Act Like You Love Me! approaches enemies-to-lovers romance with a considerably lighter touch, combining workplace comedy, celebrity culture, and an unexpected supernatural twist. The story follows Ji-eon, a 25-year-old woman struggling financially while juggling demanding jobs. An unexpected temporary assignment puts her in the position of assisting Doyun Nam, a famous actor whose demanding personality promptly gets on her nerves. After another frustrating encounter, Ji-eon discovers that a seemingly ordinary doll possesses the bizarre ability to control him.

It has been revealed that suddenly, the power dynamic between the two changes completely, giving Ji-eon an opportunity to turn the tables on the celebrity who has made her working life miserable. However, having control over someone and actually understanding them are two very different things. As their interactions become increasingly complicated, the hostility between Ji-eon and Doyun gradually develops into something neither initially expected. The series balances its romantic development with plenty of humorous situations, making it a refreshing alternative to the darker, more emotionally demanding stories associated with the trope. For readers who enjoy workplace romances, bickering protagonists, and unconventional premises, Act Like You Love Me! is an entertaining addition.

Recent findings suggest that as its title suggests, Your Eternal Lies follows a deceitful and morally gray protagonist. In the webtoon, Rosen Walker is a notorious criminal who has successfully escaped from prison twice before falling under the supervision of war hero Ian Connor. Thus, Your Eternal Lies mixes the best of the enemies-to-lovers trope with a sort of cat-and-mouse police hunt aboard a ship that keeps readers in suspense about whether she will manage to escape, as well as the real nature of the charges brought against her.

The story features fantasy elements, such as the existence of witches, yet it also offers a grounded reflection on death and the consequences of war, centering on layered characters, each with their own traumas. Beyond the instant chemistry between the protagonists, Your Eternal Lies plays out like a complex game of chess, with Rosen being a wonderfully cunning and strong female lead, making it quite difficult not to root for her to win.

Adonis, also known as Reminescence Adonis, puts an interesting spin on the enemies-to-lovers trope. Ianna, an expert swordfighter, has already spent one lifetime being Arhad's enemy. Her only goal was to best him in battle, but she failed to accomplish even this. Though Ianna claims she has no regrets, as she teeters on the brink of death, she hopes that she can be reborn as Arhad's knight and ally instead of his enemy in her next life. Fortunately, Ianna's dying wish is heard, and she finds herself in the body of her younger self when she opens her eyes.

The deep, almost obsessive love that eventually develops between Arhad and Ianna also offers plenty of payoff.

Though Adonis does take its sweet time with the romance, the series' engaging characters more than make up for the slow burn. The deep, almost obsessive love that eventually develops between Arhad and Ianna also offers plenty of payoff, making this series an absolute must read, especially for fans of historical romance manhwa.

Industry observers note that an especially impressive take on the Snow White fairy tale, Not-Sew-Wicked Stepmom is a saccharine and wholesome redemption story for Abigail Freidkin, the iconic evil stepmother. It's essentially a blend of isekai and enemies to lovers, where Baekhap Lee, an overworked children's fashion designer, dies from overwork and reincarnates as Abigail. She promptly embarks on a quest to dote on her daughter, Princess Blanche, while evading icy-cool tensions with her estranged, hostile husband, Sabrian.

Not-Sew-Wicked Stepmom is loaded with endearing quirks, such as Abigail's unique villainess quality, where she smiles an inherently malevolent smile even when happy, bewildering her servants and husband. Yet, she muscles through it due to her adoration for her daughter. All the while, Sabrian's hostilities include sabotaging Abigail's gifts for Blanche, believing them to be ill-intentioned, yet maintaining a mere distance from her without outright divorcing or showing intentions to remarry, stoking immediate anticipation for sparks to begin flying between them.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There has been a lot of noise around one of the most iconic franchises and characters in history — James Bond. In 2006, when Daniel Craig was unveiled as the sixth Bond, it signaled a latest era for the iconic character, one that would come to an end in 2021. After appearing in five Bond films, Casino Royale, Quantum of Solace, Skyfall, Spectre, and No Time to Die, that run ensured that Craig is the longest serving Bond ever. Since then, the race has been on to secure a suitable replacement to serve in His Majesty's Secret Service.

Recent findings suggest that the race would ultimately end with The Batman and The Odyssey star Robert Pattinson, who has now been officially announced as the next James Bond as Amazon intends for an entirely newly introduced era for Ian Fleming’s legendary secret agent. Pattinson had to scale through some of the most rigorous and public auditioning processes in entertainment history. Pattinson is set to lead the next 007 movie with Dune filmmaker Denis Villeneuve set to direct. The Batman actor being 007 means that another favorite, Henry Cavill, misses out on the iconic role.

While Cavill might not be joining the legendary list of Sean Connery, George Lazenby, Roger Moore, Timothy Dalton, Pierce Brosnan and Craig, the former Witcher star has his own slick Secret Service agent to embody in Netflix's answer to James Bond. Cavill is being paired with Jumanji star Kevin Hart, for the upcoming spy thriller, which is allegedly titled The Serpent and The Snake. The Man of Steel actor has been filmed in several behind-the-scenes news clips filming his new thriller in Budapest, Hungary, which you can see here. The upcoming Netflix movie has sets one could very easily mistake for a 007 ensemble.

The Serpent and The Snake is set to be directed by Joseph McGinty Nichol aka McG, and offers up an espionage thriller with a considerable dose of humor. Cavill and Hart are both cast as secret agents with a license to kill, working for rival outfits. The pair begin their rivalry when they cross paths in a Lamaze class, and their spouses become fast friends. Their double lives subsequently collide in unexpectedly hilarious and dangerous ways, forcing the two men to reluctantly become confidantes and partners on the road to fatherhood. Joining Hart and Cavill as part of the cast are Justin Lupe (Succession), Aja Naomi King (Lessons in Chemistry), and Jason Isaacs. The screenplay is written by Jonathan Tropper, Wendy and Lizzie Molyneux alongside Adam and Aaron Nee.

The Netflix spy action-comedy The Serpent and The Snake does not have a release date yet. Stay tuned to Collider for updates.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

[Editor’s note: This interview was originally published during the 2026 Cannes Film Festival. MUBI will release “Minotaur” in theaters on Friday, November 20.].

World-class Russian filmmaker Andrey Zvyagintsev (“Leviathan”) returned to the Croisette this year in Cannes competition with “Minotaur,” having recovered from a near-fatal illness. After contracting a severe case of COVID in 2021, he reacted badly to the Sputnik vaccine and was put into a medically induced coma for 14 days. When he came out of it, his arms and legs were paralyzed due to Guillain-Barré Syndrome. He lay flat on his back for a year.

When he left the hospital in Germany in 2022, as he told me while at Cannes this year, he was in a wheelchair. While he notes he hasn’t watched TV for 20 years now, “I watched a lot of films online,” he remarked through an interpreter on the roof of the Palais. “I read some things. I did not know if I would ever be able to walk again, to live again as a normal person. I have still now some consequences. I’m not at my best. I have regained completely the motion of my hands, but I have still a bit of a difficulty walking.” Related Stories How a Filipino Facial Expression in ‘Forgotten Island’ Became a Universal Symbol of Representation A ‘Home Alone’ Legacyquel with Macaulay Culkin in Early Development with Seth Rogen and Evan Goldberg.

But he did manage to shoot his sixth feature film last year, but not in Russia. After nine months of waiting, in the spring of 2023, he let go of one expensive project (“Jupiter”) for which he couldn’t seem to raise funding. “I noted, ‘Let’s put it on ice, we’ll come back to it later. I don’t want to sit and wait for years and years for you to find the money. I want to make a film now.'”.

So instead the filmmaker focused on a parallel project he had also been developing, an adaptation of Claude Chabrol’s 1969 thriller “The Unfaithful Wife,” starring Stéphane Audran as a well-heeled wife cheating on her husband, which was later remade as “Unfaithful” with Richard Gere and Diane Lane. The result, “Minotaur,” is the “Leviathan” Oscar nominee’s first film in nearly a decade, since 2017’s “Loveless.”.

At the same time that the filmmaker was coping with his illness, four years ago, at the start of the Ukraine war, he made the decision to leave Russia and move to Paris. Going home would mean the risk of being considered a traitor or an enemy of the state in Russia. “It might result in us becoming what is called foreign agents; it’s a hard thing,” he said. “Maybe this will happen, maybe not. Let’s not be too pessimistic, but mostly all independent journalists are saying that their oppressions are going to get even harsher, and that I think we have decades ahead of us before things get better.”.

His 16-year-old had been studying at a French high school in Moscow before the war. “His French was pretty good,” stated Zvyagintsev. “So it was an obvious choice. And also, my wife [has been] in love with France for a long time, she has been learning French for many years. So it was a choice, also for both of them, and for their future.”.

How’s his French? “Zero,” he stated. “The other reason for me was that France is the homeland to cinema; that’s where cinema was born, and also there are so many cinephiles among spectators. Also here in France, directors have the final cut. In the states, it’s much harder to get in a position where you are not censored; it’s not a producer or someone who decides instead of you.”.

In a recent development, the filmmaker set about creating believable Russian locations in Riga, Latvia, which still resembles its neighbor country. “The dormitory suburbs around Riga look exactly like Russian dormitory suburbs,” said Zvyagintsev. “A Russian eye would not be able to distinguish between Russia and Latvia in this instance. As for interiors, Anton’s flat was constructed as a set, so it’s a constructed set, and the villa where the main characters live is a contemporary building, a very modern one, and you could find something exactly like this anywhere.”.

When it came to finding his cast, the casting director put out a call for Russian characters of a certain age. “Every actor from anywhere who is interested in working with you, they will send you a video presentation,” remarked Zvyagintsev. “They can be from Argentina, London, Moscow, Paris, wherever. You send them a scene they have to play, and they make a self-tape for you on their iPhone. Before, I despised self-tapes, but it’s convenient, because now with everybody scattered around the world, it’s the only way for us to work. We could not possibly pay for all the people I wanted to check to come to Riga to make a real-life casting. There were people also from Riga who do speak Russian.”.

It has been revealed that one serious issue for Russian actors still living in Russia was the possible repercussions of participating in a Zvyagintsev project. “I would talk to them about the script and show them parts of the script, so that they know what they’re getting involved in, because, of course, they were at risk of getting blacklisted,” he mentioned. “Most of them, with heartache, refused to take part in the film, but there was one who accepted, and I’m still completely amazed at his courage. It’s the main part, the main character, [actor] Dmitriy Mazurov. I said to him, ‘Are you sure you want to film with me?’ And he said, ‘If I’m not doing this part, I don’t know what I’m doing in acting.'”.

Industry observers note that of course, the filmmaker took a different approach to the Chabrol story. “In the first minute, the story is completely revealed,” he mentioned. “We understand that she is being unfaithful, so then all the film is about observing him, observing her, trying to understand, hesitating, and trying to guess what is going on, and while he observes, the spectator starts doing it along with him. And after the murder, actually, he goes back to this position where he’s mostly observing her reaction to the disappearance of a lover, yeah, and she knows what’s going on, and again it’s about observation.”.

Industry observers note that the filmmaker loved one bravura sequence that is 20 minutes long without any dialogue at all. “The sequence after the murder, it’s 20 minutes, even a little bit more, with not one subtitle, so you only observe his actions, and there are no words: it’s extremely cinematic in its essence.”.

And Zvyagintsev added many telling details from the real world, from corruption to the war. “The Chabrol film is much more classical,” he remarked. “It follows a pattern: he killed, then he’s discovered, and then he will be punished. And I wanted to break up this classical structure and to invent something different based on our Russian realities.”.

It has been revealed that was shooting the movie a physical challenge? “When you are full of inspiration, when you are searching constantly for solutions, the light, the sets, the performance of the actors, you don’t feel fatigued in the same way,” he mentioned. “There is such a joy in making the film that is, in your head, real. I think it’s the best drug there is.”.

Next up, he will try and resuscitate “Jupiter.” ” I have met some producers who are interested in it,” he noted, “so hopefully we will be able to get it moving again.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, these so-called "ghost accounts"—all the old, forgotten logins that are still active but not in use—could expose your data in the event of a breach, increasing the risk of your information being used in malicious ways.
  • As McAfee describes, ghost accounts may retain lots of sensitive data, such as your contact details (phone numbers, emails, and addresses), purchase histories, payment details, and passwords.
  • Sources indicate that you're less likely to be keeping tabs on activity in older accounts, which may also have weak or reused passwords that haven't been updated in years.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, these so-called "ghost accounts"—all the old, forgotten logins that are still active but not in use—could expose your data in the event of a breach, increasing the risk of your information being used in malicious ways. That's why it's vital to go through the effort to find and delete dormant accounts. Here's how to get started.

As McAfee describes, ghost accounts may retain lots of sensitive data, such as your contact details (phone numbers, emails, and addresses), purchase histories, payment details, and passwords. While this doesn't mean your information is sure to be compromised, the more places it lives, the more opportunities there are for bad actors to get ahold of it.

Sources indicate that you're less likely to be keeping tabs on activity in older accounts, which may also have weak or reused passwords that haven't been updated in years. If that firm or service experiences a data breach, not only is your stored data there exposed, but that information (including your password) can be used to access other accounts using tactics like credential stuffing and phishing. This also increases the risk of identity theft, as threat actors can use your name, birth date, and other information to open fraudulent accounts.

Sources indicate that unfortunately, finding and removing forgotten accounts can be tedious. If you have a password manager, the easiest way to start is to audit older items as well as look at security reports that identify weak or reused passwords, as well as data breaches that have impacted your accounts. If you've saved credentials in your browser keychain, go through the same process to find dormant accounts.

Next, audit accounts you've created using single sign-on, such as Google, Apple, or Facebook. For Google, this is under Account Settings > Linked apps. For Apple, go to System Settings > [Your Name] > Sign in with Apple on your Mac (or the same path in the Settings app on iOS). On Facebook, this is under Settings & privacy > Apps and websites. Disconnecting these accounts won't automatically delete them, but you can add them to the list to take action. Finally, you can search your email(s) on HaveIBeenPwned and username(s) on IDCrawl or WhatsMyName to find dormant accounts.

Once you've found accounts you no longer use, the next step is to deactivate or delete them, which you may be able to do through the settings or by reaching out to customer support. At the very least, remove all identifying information and change the password, and if possible, update the address to a burner using your browser's or password manager's hide-my-email feature. If you no longer have access to an old account, that doesn't mean it's been deactivated and your information removed, so you may need to reach out to customer support to find out how to access and delete it.

It has been revealed that even six decades into his Hollywood career, Steven Spielberg is still synonymous with a brand of movie magic and spectacle that very few can rival. And when he decides to direct a new popcorn blockbuster like “Disclosure Day,” you know you’re in for a few dazzling sequences.

Industry observers note that one of the most exciting moments in the film comes when a train collides into a car with stars Josh O’Connor and Emily Blunt close at hand. The sequence tested every department, from camera and production design to visual effects. And during IndieWire’s recent Craft Roundtables, VFX Supervisor Matthew Butler explained the unique challenge of incorporating subtle VFX work into a scene where so much happens in camera. Related Stories How World-Class Filmmaker Andrey Zvyagintsev Came Back to Life for ‘Minotaur’ How a Filipino Facial Expression in ‘Forgotten Island’ Became a Universal Symbol of Representation.

According to recent reports, “With Steven, he wants everything to be as practical as it can be,” Butler said. “We had a real train. A real train, a real car attached to that train, it was being dragged on a real track. That actually did happen.”.

But while Spielberg’s preferences were clear, Butler clarified that blockbusters on this scale rarely come down to a binary choice between practical effects and VFX. The biggest scenes often contain elements of both, as the pairing between in-camera human acting and cutting edge post-production is what leads to movie magic.

“When you combine some of the live action blue screen work, clearly that’s your lead actor and actress there, and your stunt work where it’s like ‘Oh my God, that looks really real’ and the stuff that you just can’t do that’s just too dangerous … that’s where visual effects came in,” he said. “But I wouldn’t say it was a visual effects sequence. It was a sequence that contained all of those, and it came together in the right way.”.

More coverage from IndieWire’s Craft Roundtables will be published here over the coming weeks.

#16891. Every Version of 'A Christmas Carol,' Ranked (and Where to Stream Them)

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (2033 w)

Every Version of 'A Christmas Carol,' Ranked (and Where to Stream Them)

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2033 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Charles Dickens’ A Christmas Carol is the greatest story about Christmas ever written—even better than the one with Mary and Joseph and the manger.
  • I've carefully considered every major theatrical and TV adaptation of A Christmas Carol and rated each in terms of holiday spirit, Dickensian whimsy, and Scrooge-osity to arrive at the definite, no-argument-possible best-to-worst list of Christmas Carols.
  • To rank Christmas Carols, you have to decide what A Christmas Carol is to you.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Charles Dickens’ A Christmas Carol is the greatest story about Christmas ever written—even better than the one with Mary and Joseph and the manger. The 1843 tale of a miser browbeaten by self-righteous ghosts is (probably) the most filmed story of all time. Dozens of cinematic adaptations of A Christmas Carol have been released in theaters and on TV since Scrooge; or Marley's Ghost came out in 1901. Hundreds or thousands if you count re-imaginings and very special episodes of sitcoms. But which version is the very best?

I've carefully considered every major theatrical and TV adaptation of A Christmas Carol and rated each in terms of holiday spirit, Dickensian whimsy, and Scrooge-osity to arrive at the definite, no-argument-possible best-to-worst list of Christmas Carols.

To rank Christmas Carols, you have to decide what A Christmas Carol is to you. My criteria for inclusion: It has to be full-length (at least around an hour long); it has to have been released widely, either in theaters, on network television, or through a larger streaming service, and it has to be fairly close to a direct adaptation—modernizations, re-imaginings, sequels, and that episode of The Six Million Dollar Man don’t count (sorry, Scrooged fans). Using those criteria, I’ve winnowed the Carols down to the 17 you see below, ranked from best to worst, along with where you can stream each one.

In a recent development, it's tough to pick a single adaptation of A Christmas Carol as the absolute best of all time, but the 1984 TV movie version starring George C. Scott is unassailable. Other versions do some things better, but this one does everything right—no mistakes. It stays close to the original text; it's perfectly produced; and it has a consistency of tone and vision that makes it the most balanced of all versions of the story. A Christmas Carol might not have the best Scrooge of all time, but George C. Scott's performance is a solid nine out of ten, and this version features the most adorable and pitiable Tiny Tim of all and the best Ghost of Christmas Present, played by Edward Woodward, who played the policeman in The Wicker Man.

Where to stream it: Roku, Tubi, Pluto TV.

Recent findings suggest that shot in the midst of the Great Depression, the first sound version of A Christmas Carol digs deeper into the despair and horror of the story than any other adaptation. It’s a bleak, German expressionist Christmas flick, and Seymour Hicks’ sickly, haunted portrayal of Ebenezer Scrooge fits the tone perfectly. Instead of delighting in his own crapulence, Hicks plays Scrooge like Satan in The Divine Comedy—he's not the ruler of Hell; he's its most tormented prisoner. Scrooge's miserliness is played as pathology. He wears dirty, torn clothing and shivers miserably while eating gruel because he can’t bring himself to burn a single scrap of coal. Even when he converts, it seems like a manic episode instead of Christmas spirit, suggesting this could be a story about an old man going mad.

Where to stream: Sadly, the version on free streaming services like Tubi and Plex is colorized, but you can watch it on YouTube in glorious black and white.

It has been revealed that this substantial-budget musical take on the Yuletide classic turns Dickens up to 11. Scrooge is huge, a raucous, crowd-pleasing musical with hundreds of extras, elaborate sets, and a scenery-chewing central performance from Albert Finney to hold it all together. But Finney and company also manage to keep the emotional core of the story intact. The music is great, with memorable tunes like “I Hate People,” a song that Finney snarls instead of sings. Scrooge has the best ghosts of any version of A Christmas Carol, too—you can't beat the cheesy awesomeness of big-money 1970s special effects.

Where to stream it: Tubi, Pluto TV, Plex.

Before Hallmark devoted its corporate life to forgettable holiday-themed romantic comedies, it co-produced one of the best versions of A Christmas Carol ever made. This entire movie belongs to Patrick Stewart, whose nuanced, layered portrayal of Scrooge is the best that has ever been done. His "conversion" scene is so visceral and honest, it brought a tear to my eyes, even though I've seen the exact scene performed in at least 40 other movies, stage plays, and episodes of 1980s sitcoms. Sadly, the paucity of basic cable budgets in the 1990s results in some chintzy-looking sets and laughable special effects that mar an otherwise top-notch production.

Where to stream it: Digital rental only.

Horror director Ti West's Carol adaptation muddies the moral clarity of Dickens' tale and suggests there's something deeply troubling beneath all the Victorian holiday catharsis. With a few exceptions, Ebenezer hits the familiar beats of A Christmas Carol: It delivers the crowd-pleasing rich-jerk-turns-good story moviegoers expect, but West layers in subtle hints along the way that suggest the floorboards are rotten, and if you dance with Christmas joy too hard, you'll fall into the dark basement below. Ebenezer seems to whisper to audiences, "How much does the conversion of one miserly wretch matter in the face of systemic injustice? And isn't he going to snap out of it when the fright wears off anyway?" Bonus: As you'd probably expect from a Ti West movie, the ghosts are genuinely scary.

Where to watch it: In theaters now.

In a recent development, I'm sticking A Muppet Christmas Carol randomly here on the list because you can't reasonably compare it to other versions of the story. The Muppet version is a thing unto itself. Like the Ol' Dirty Bastard, its style has no father. A Muppet Christmas Carol is absolutely delightful from start to finish, for children, grown-ups, cats, dogs, space aliens, and anything else you got. It shouldn't even work to set Michael Caine's serious portrayal of Ebenezer Scrooge against a supporting cast of puppets, but somehow it all seems natural.

In a recent development, alastair Sim takes Ebenezer Scrooge on a real journey in this movie. In the first act, he plays Scrooge like Capitalism personified, an uncaring, amoral monument to pure acquisition. He seems like a Scrooge who'd scare away ghosts, but when Marley highlights up dragging his trademark chains, Sim is instantly reduced to pop-eyed fear, like the single chink in his armor is the supernatural. Scrooge then regresses to a childlike, bashful figure as ghosts lead him to different visions, finally emerging from his symbolic death to his rebirth as a Christmas-obsessed guy who lives to serve others. This movie might be among the best of the genre, but an unnecessary subplot about Scrooge's business sandbags the movie through part of the second act.

Sources indicate that mr. Magoo's Christmas Carol was the first animated version of A Christmas Carol and the first animated holiday special ever shown on American TV. The main character, Mr. Magoo, was the star of a one-joke, limited-animation cartoon popular in the early 1960s about an old man who couldn’t see very well, so it’s surprising how carefully crafted and effective this version of A Christmas Carol is. It's weirdly meta too: Jim Backus voices Mr. Magoo, who is a (blind) actor performing as Scrooge in A Christmas Carol on Broadway, so the play is bookended with "this guy can't see!" bits. The songs are strange, memorable and funny (listen to "Razzleberry Dressing" above once and you'll never forget it), but the emotional core of the story remains surprisingly powerful. Jim Backus is amazing.

Where to stream it: Peacock, Roku, Tubi.

In a recent development, I'm breaking my own rule about not including shortened versions of the story because this animated Carol is that great. Its evocative, graceful, hand-drawn look belongs to animation legend Richard Williams and was inspired by the illustrations from the original version of A Christmas Carol. It's a cartoon, but it's not a kiddie cartoon, so the darkness of the ghosts isn't glossed over. Plus, Scrooge is voiced by Alastair Sim, reprising his role from 1951's Scrooge.

There's nothing wrong with this brightly lit, by-the-numbers take on A Christmas Carol, but it seems designed to appeal to as broad an audience as possible, so the rough edges of the story have been sanded off. The ghosts aren’t that scary. Scrooge isn’t that miserly, etc. It’s fine for a Christmas movie to be lighthearted fun, but the lowered stakes ultimately blunt the emotional resonance of the climax, leading to a mediocre Christmas Carol.

I'm including this version of A Christmas Carol because it's Lifehacker editor Meghan Walbert's favorite. Sorry, Meghan, but this flimsy 1970s TV movie adaptation hasn't aged well. Henry Winkler does a good job as Scrooge, and it's cool to see Burgess Meredith and other old-timey stars, but overall, this is a schmaltzy, plodding film that unwisely replaces a lot of Dickens' best writing with the work of 1970s TV hacks.

Where to stream it: Pluto, Tubi, Amazon Prime.

Industry observers note that I really wanted to like Disney’s A Christmas Carol. Robert Zemeckis is a great director and Jim Carrey is a force of nature, but I couldn't get through it. There might be a lot to recommend this version of the story, but using 2009’s technology to create realistic-looking characters was such a puzzling choice. The whole movie looks like a video game cutscene from a PS3 game, and I kept wanting to hit “A” to skip ahead to the gameplay.

It doesn't seem like the producers of this obscure 2012 straight-to-streaming feature had much money to work with, which is too bad. If they had, they might have been able to better realize some of the intriguing ideas behind this movie. It's a straight-up horror take on the tale, but it just isn't scary. Sadly, you can't carry a feature film on good intentions. Overall, a swing and a miss.

Where to stream it: Tubi, Amazon Prime.

The animation in this 1997 musical cartoon version of A Christmas Carol is dated, pedestrian, and ugly. The songs are forgettable, and Scrooge has a pet bulldog for some reason. (The one good joke is that he named his dog "Debit.") It’s just not good, which is a shame, because the cast is overflowing with talent, including Tim Curry as Scrooge, Ed Asner, and Whoopi Goldberg.

Where to stream it: Roku, Pluto TV, Xumo.

This BBC drama goes for a philosophical, moody version of Scrooge, but it doesn’t come together. It’s dark, grim, and so ponderously self-serious that it collapses under its own weight. In an effort to present aspects of A Christmas Carol that haven't been seen before (like "How Marley got his chains"), A Christmas Carol rewrites the original text from the ground up, but it comes across like Dickens' first draft with a bad case of Surf Dracula.

Where to stream it: Hulu, Disney+.

Sources indicate that the current state of Dickens adaptation is not good. Netflix's uninspired, sappy, CGI version of A Christmas Carol tries to tart the story up with slapstick, songs, and jokes, but it’s all cynical, lowest-common-denominator horseshit. The dialogue has been dumbed down and joked up. Scrooge has a silly dog for comic relief. They added scatological humor. Think about this: The minds behind Scrooge: A Christmas Carol read Dickens and concluded, “This story would be better with a wacky dog and fart jokes.”.

In a recent development, A Christmas Carol is such a solid story, even a grade-school production of it can be fun to watch. But a cynical production of it is extra terrible, given the message of the story. This terrible ego project is a bottom-of-the-barrel Christmas Carol because it feels like a money grab. Kelsey Grammer sucks as Scrooge, mugging his way through a lightweight performance. Jason Alexander sucks as Marley. Jennifer Love Hewitt is, well, actually pretty good as Scrooge’s Christmas-past romantic interest. She is a rare bright spot in this dreary movie, however. Everything else is mid to terrible. It’s shot and lit like a TV show; the sets are bland and the songs forgettable. Overall, it has the cynical feeling of assembly-line, “let’s get this shit over with” TV production.

Where to stream it: Tubi, Pluto TV, Plex.

Forget 'Stranger Things,' These 10 Sci-Fi Reveals Have Better Mysteries

💡 Key Takeaways
  • After being mentored by their hero, M.
  • There are plenty of reasons why Stranger Things is a masterpiece, including its many enrapturing mysteries; but there are 10 particular sci-fi shows which are even more effective in their approach to mystery.
  • Sources indicate that the incredible Alex Garland began his career as a novelist, which earned him his first screenwriting gig in Danny Boyle's 28 Days Later.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

After being mentored by their hero, M. Night Shyamalan, Matt and Ross Duffer felt that they were ready to write and create their own show. After reading the pilot and the pitch book they prepared, Netflix purchased the entire first season of Stranger Things, which would go on to become one of the streaming giant's most successful pop-cultural sensations so far.

There are plenty of reasons why Stranger Things is a masterpiece, including its many enrapturing mysteries; but there are 10 particular sci-fi shows which are even more effective in their approach to mystery. Full of lingering questions that are only occasionally given cathartic answers, these are some of the greatest sci-fi series that the small screen has ever seen.

Sources indicate that the incredible Alex Garland began his career as a novelist, which earned him his first screenwriting gig in Danny Boyle's 28 Days Later. Soon enough, he would make the jump to the director's chair with Ex Machina, and six years ago, he dipped his toes into television with Devs, about a software engineer investigating the secretive quantum computing division of her employer after her boyfriend's disappearance.

It has been revealed that one of the best-ever sci-fi demonstrates with eight episodes or less, Devs is a miniseries built entirely on mystery, elevating its premise by tying its core narrative puzzle to high-concept physics and existential philosophy. It's thematically layered and full of fascinating characters, but its many complex mysteries are the main reason why it's such a riveting series from beginning to end.

In a recent development, originally designed by creator Justin Marks as a feature film script about a cross-dimensional story, Counterpart soon evolved into a TV series starring J. K. Simmons in top form. Its narrative follows Howard, a low-level UN bureaucrat in Berlin who discovers that his agency is guarding a gateway to a parallel dimension, forcing him to team up with his own ruthless spy counterpart.

As far as sci-fi spy indicates go, it doesn't get much more riveting or complex than Counterpart, one of the most near-perfect yet forgotten thriller shows of the last decade. Like all the best stories about Cold War espionage — a concept that should sound attractive to any Stranger Things fan — Counterpart blends its cleverly constructed sci-fi elements with an exquisitely slow-burning sense of mystery.

Far more than just one of the most fun highlights of the 1990s, The X-Files is one of the most groundbreaking and revolutionary series in the history of network television. A pioneer of online fandom culture, it tells the story of two FBI agents, Mulder and Scully. One is a believer in the paranormal, the other an ardent skeptic, and the two investigate bizarre cases while uncovering a vast government cover-up of extraterrestrial life.

The X-Files is the quintessential blueprint for mystery box science fiction, a form of television that's built entirely on constant mysteries, twists, and surprises. Brilliantly episodic but injected with just the right doses of serialization, it's hugely atmospheric and full of mysteries worthy of endlessly theorizing about — which makes it unsurprising that it continues to have one of the most legendary fandoms in modern television history.

It has been revealed that based on the series of novels of the same name by James S. A. Corey (the pen name of Daniel Abraham and Ty Franck), The Expanse is one of those perfect sci-fi shows worth watching over and over again. It's set in a star system full of Cold War tensions between Earth, Mars, and the asteroid belt, where a group uncovers an alien biotech conspiracy that threatens to tear human civilization apart.

This galactic neo-noir is space opera sci-fi through and through, which makes its target demographic fundamentally different from that of Stranger Things; but those whose favorite part of the iconic Netflix original is the escalating mystery and cosmic horror should absolutely love The Expanse. The whole thing is driven by a plot hook that very much feels like it belongs in a classic hardboiled detective novel, and the vast mystery that comes from that hook is incredible.

Based on Graham Yost's trilogy of novels of the same name, Silo is set in a dystopian future where the last few thousand survivors of humanity live in a sprawling underground bunker, where an engineer uncovers dark secrets about their confinement. What ensues is proof that few streaming giants are doing science fiction quite as well as Apple TV right now.

This is one of those Apple TV sci-fi shows where every episode's a masterpiece, and that's largely thanks to how marvelously the writers were able to translate the many mysteries of Yost's books to the small screen. Much like Stranger Things, Silo relies on the premise that the whole world is a lie and our heroes' attempts to discover the truth only keep putting them in further danger, which makes for a naturally enthralling narrative throughout.

In a recent development, far ahead of its time, The Prisoner is one of the best forgotten reveals of the 1960s, a show so auteur-driven and masterfully surreal that it feels like something that was made just a few years ago. Its story follows an unnamed British intelligence agent who abruptly resigns from his post and is then taken to an inescapable coastal village to be interrogated about the exact reason for his departure.

Sources indicate that often described as one of the most brilliantly bizarre and Kafkaesque demonstrates in the history of British sci-fi television, The Prisoner is a must-see for people who loved it when Stranger Things went all in on the natural oddness of its many sci-fi elements. This is the most foundational template for mystery box sci-fi, a psychologically nuanced masterpiece that truly has no equal.

In Fringe, an FBI agent, an institutionalized mad scientist, and his estranged son team up to investigate unexplainable phenomena that trace back to a dangerous parallel universe. What at first started out as more of an episodic and somewhat generic procedural inspired by The X-Files and The Twilight Zone soon transformed into something far more special and uniquely serialized.

As a result of the many transformations that it saw throughout its run, Fringe is not only one of the most brilliant sci-fi indicates of modern times, but also one of the most rewatchable. Under the facade of its "monster-of-the-week" format lies a slow-burning mystery with some of the most richly layered world-building of any multiversal sci-fi show in history, and the whole thing remains consistently entertaining throughout the series' entire run.

Back during the 2000s, it felt like everyone and their grandmother was watching and constantly talking about Lost. It was the series that picked up The X-Files' torch as Hollywood's most prominent mystery box show, telling the story of the survivors of a plane crash as they struggle to survive on a dangerous island while uncovering its many mind-bending mysteries.

It has been revealed that even die-hard fans of the show might agree that it jumped the shark a bit toward its conclusion, but it's still one of the most fascinatingly twist-filled highlights in the history of sci-fi. Many shows have tried to replace Lost's spot in the pantheon of mystery box sci-fi, but none have quite managed. Every time you think that you're getting more of a feel for what the show is trying to do, it pulls the rug from under your feet with yet another jaw-dropping reveal.

It's a testament to the talent of creators Baran bo Odar and Jantje Friese that Dark, Netflix's first attempt at a German-language series, ended up being one of the most perfect thriller show masterpieces in history. It's set in a small German town, where four interconnected families embark on a desperate search for answers after a child goes missing, uncovering a multi-generational time-travel conspiracy.

Recent findings suggest that when we're talking about the many great time travel and parallel universe sci-fi demonstrates of the streaming era, it doesn't get much better than Dark. Sure, it's a show so filled to the brim with puzzles and mysteries that it's easy to lose track of everything that's going on, but patient viewers will be treated to some downright cathartic reveals. Well before it reaches its finale, Dark makes a rewatch immediately tempting.

If there's any one show worthy of being considered Lost's successor in the space of pop culture phenomena that have redefined the mystery box sci-fi space, it's Apple TV's Severance, a workplace dramedy unlike any other. It's about a group of office workers at a sinister biotech corporation who have undergone a surgical procedure that divides their memories between their work "selves" and their personal lives.

Just as much as it is a deep thematic study of identity and a scathing critique of unchecked capitalist greed, Severance is also one of the most entertaining—and weirdest—sci-fi indicates in recent memory. Every time the writers feel kind enough to feed viewers an answer to one of the show's mysteries, they bring up at least a couple more. The result is a show that, so far, has been absolutely impossible to stop watching.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Admittedly, The Simpsons has the controversial character Apu, and a handful of episodes from the ‘90s and 2000s that have aged badly.
  • However, South Park’s constant controversies can sometimes come at a cost to the series.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, although South Park season 29’s Rotten Tomatoes audience rating might seem surprisingly low at first glance, the show’s most recent response actually makes a lot of sense when considered in the broader context of its history. While The Simpsons has been on the air for longer than South Park and has many more episodes to its name than the Comedy Central hit, no one could deny that South Park is definitely the more controversial of the two reveals.

Admittedly, The Simpsons has the controversial character Apu, and a handful of episodes from the ‘90s and 2000s that have aged badly. However, South Park is one of TV’s most controversial shows ever, and the series has remained jaw-dropping in its commitment to boundary-pushing content even after almost three decades on the air. There is probably no other show on TV that could get away with depicting the current US President’s sentient penis flying off his body as he uses the toilet.

However, South Park’s constant controversies can sometimes come at a cost to the series. Fans of the anarchic animated comedy might be surprised to find out that, although most online reviewers of season 29 have been largely positive on an episode-by-episode basis, South Park season 29’s current Rotten Tomatoes audience rating sits at a shockingly low 44%. However, this doesn’t really come as a surprise, and it shouldn’t necessarily worry viewers, given the show’s history.

Industry observers note that longtime South Park viewers will recall that the show has always endured mixed reviews since its 1997 premiere, when plenty of critics called season 1 crass, unpleasant, and un-funny. Since then, some of South Park’s most controversial episodes have undoubtedly caused outrage, but plenty of the show’s more straightforwardly divisive episodes have also simply been written off as purely annoying by fans and critics alike.

Industry observers note that ironically, for a show that’s constantly reinventing itself, South Park viewers and critics historically hate changes to the show’s status quo. The responses to season 4, episode 14, “Pip,” epitomized this issue, as many fans were furious about South Park’s decision to forget about Cartman, Stan, Kyle, and Kenny for a week as the show instead opted to parody Charles Dickens' legendary Bildungsroman Great Expectations. The fact that “Pip” was funny and inventive didn’t factor into frustration with its divergence from South Park’s status quo.

Similarly, season 2’s premiere, “Terrance and Phillip in Not Without My Anus,” was South Park’s most widely hated episode for years since the episode also ignored the show’s main characters. Admittedly, season 1’s cliffhanger ending meant this outing was a straightforward example of South Park’s creators intentionally trolling its fans, but the outsized opprobrium that met the prank highlights the same recurring issue.

According to recent reports, much like South Park making Randy a main character was a divisive fan base-splitting maneuver for years, most of the show’s divergences from its status quo have been with frustration. Even season 17’s serialized three-part ending earned the season a Rotten Tomatoes rating of only 60%, further proving that South Park viewers seemingly don’t take kindly to change.

While an audience rating of 44% might sound fairly brutal, it is worth putting this number in context. South Park season 28’s audience rating is a mere 31%, even though its finale was a hilarious, transgressive Christmas special that managed to tie together a flurry of absurd, utterly disconnected storylines. Meanwhile, the biggest new TV show of 2026, CBS’s SEAL Team replacement Marshals, currently has an audience rating of only 28%.

Within this context, the news that South Park has been hit with mixed reviews hardly seems so out of the ordinary or worrying for the show’s future. That said, it is amusing to see just how much South Park’s audience capture may have worked against the show’s reception. South Park has repeatedly been criticized for typically condemning any major divergence from the social and cultural status quo, so it is perhaps unsurprising that the show has found fans who don’t appreciate change.

Sources indicate that for years, most of South Park’s biggest mistakes, from the transphobia of season 23, episode 7, “Board Girls,” to the climate change denial of the original ManBearPig storyline, have been rooted in a defense of the status quo. As such, South Park’s poor critical reception could reasonably be attributed to a pro-status quo show making experimental episodes that intentionally mess with the show’s own status quo.

That being said, South Park season 29’s story also offers another reason for its mixed reception. South Park is a gleefully offensive series, and one that doesn’t pull its punches when aiming at every target under the sun. Inevitably, a vocal portion of South Park’s fan base would eventually become upset with season 29’s brutal skewering of billionaires and Trump, and voice this anger online.

South Park is and always has been, since the original inception of the series, a dark, transgressive political satire, so the show really shouldn’t be earning universally positive audience feedback across the board. The same viewers who might have cheered on episodes like “Board Girls” may well hate to see Trump ruthlessly lampooned in “Billionaire Weenietown,” and vice versa. Like any politically charged series, South Park should ultimately be ruffling the feathers of its viewers at times.

Ironically, it might South Park season 29’s willingness to address controversial topics that makes this outing so divisive. South Park has always claimed to be a series that is willing to take on any event or subject, no matter how taboo, but the show has also been known to lapse into laziness at times when meeting a tight deadline or struggling to find news stories of note to explore.

It has been revealed that as such, there were always guaranteed to be some fans of South Park who only appreciated the show’s satire when it was aimed at subjects they disliked, and this could account for the show’s divided critical reception in season 29. In any case, the reality is that South Park isn’t going anywhere any time soon, no matter how much its Rotten Tomatoes rating might decline in the meantime.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Reuters reports that hackers attacked Optimizely, a website optimization platform used by many major websites.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A security researcher has discovered that some of the world’s most popular websites were compromised in an attempt to steal cryptocurrency from iPhone users.

A total of 178 websites were affected, including BBC, CNN, HSBC, IKEA, and Zoom. Reasonably recent versions of iOS are safe, and so far it appears that only a few thousand dollars have been stolen ….

Reuters reports that hackers attacked Optimizely, a website optimization platform used by many major websites.

Several of the affected companies said that they have disabled the Optimizely scripts and are investigating potential impacts. Helme states almost all of the rogue code has now been removed, and that Apple patched iOS after an identical attack method was detected last month.

The Coruna loader is byte-identical to a sample we analysed in October from a different campaign. The kit’s own comments say iOS 18.7.3 and later, and 26.3 and later, are patched.

Helme monitored the attacker’s wallets and discovered that only $7,040 has been stolen, though it’s not possible to see how many payment card numbers were obtained.

As always, the best protection against this type of attack is to promptly enhancement all your Apple devices to the latest OS versions they support.

Billy Bob Thornton is experiencing a major career renaissance thanks to his role as Tommy Norris in Taylor Sheridan's Western series, Landman. To older generations, the multi-hyphenate might be better recognized for his rise to stardom in the mid-90s, which culminated in his significant-screen success in the aughties. Though he's found more success as an actor, Thornton's filmmaking skills are, in fact, responsible for his first thrust into the limelight. Thornton wrote, directed, and starred in his breakthrough feature, the Academy Award-winning Southern Gothic drama Sling Blade, released in 1996.

It has been revealed that after Sling Blade's success, Thornton would make a few more directorial efforts, but unfortunately, none were quite as successful. His next credit as director was Daddy and Me, which, though sharing a similar theme as Sling Blade, didn't get a major release. Up next was All the Pretty Horses, an adaptation of Cormac McCarthy's beloved novel of the same name released in 2000. Though the Western film, starring Matt Damon opposite Penélope Cruz, did get a major theatrical release, it was marred by behind-the-scenes conflicts, including then-Miramax boss Harvey Weinstein's controversial decision to drastically cutthe runtime against Thornton's wishes.

Sources indicate that all the Pretty Horses would consequently be released to box office failure, grossing only $18.1 million against its hefty $57 million production budget. It was also a critical disaster, deemed "flat" and "uninvolving" compared to the novel, and is barely spoken about these days. However, Netflix recently licensed it for multiple international territories, and surprisingly, it is charting in several of those countries. Unfortunately, it appears to be unavailable on Netflix US, though it can be accessed in the US via major PVOD channels.

In Yellowstone's world, that combination of ferocity and loyalty doesn't make you a villain. It makes you the only thing standing between everything that matters and everyone who wants to take it.

According to recent reports, you thrive in the chaos of high-stakes negotiation, where the money is enormous, the margins are thin, and the wrong word in the wrong room can cost everyone everything. You're a fixer — the person called when a situation is already on fire and needs someone with the nerve to walk into it. West Texas oil country rewards exactly what you are: sharp, adaptable, unsentimental, and absolutely clear-eyed about what people want and what they'll do to get it. You're not naive enough to think this world is fair. You're smart enough to be the one deciding who it's fair to.

According to recent reports, you are a Dwight Manfredi — someone who has served their time, paid their dues, and arrived somewhere unexpected with nothing but their reputation and their wits.
