#16879. Why Do AI Posters All Look Like That?

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1315 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Lifehacker ↗ Open Full Page

Why Do AI Posters All Look Like That?

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1315 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Every poster for a business or event has pictures of uncanny-looking people, buildings that don’t look right, and always that one font.
  • It has been revealed that at this point, gone are the days of chatbots like ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini simply generating text immediately in response to a prompt.
  • In a recent development, to borrow a classic and implausible example, if you were to give an AI chatbot the instruction “Make a peanut butter and jelly sandwich,” it would start by generating step-by-step instructions on how to make the sandwich before trying to make one (if it could).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

You know “the look” by now. Every poster for a business or event has pictures of uncanny-looking people, buildings that don’t look right, and always that one font. But why? If generative AI is supposedly able to “think” and be “creative,” why do so many of its results come out looking exactly the same? The answer is complicated, and it has to do with what chatbots define as “thinking.”.

It has been revealed that at this point, gone are the days of chatbots like ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini simply generating text immediately in response to a prompt. Some very fast models do, but most employ what’s known as “thinking models”, which are a bit of a misnomer. The “thinking” really just consists of generating a set of sub-prompts before executing the main one. And it’s in that hidden, generated text that most of the “choices” (to the extent that we can call the statistical output of an AI model a “choice”) occur that determine how a design looks.

In a recent development, to borrow a classic and implausible example, if you were to give an AI chatbot the instruction “Make a peanut butter and jelly sandwich,” it would start by generating step-by-step instructions on how to make the sandwich before trying to make one (if it could). Most of this happens invisibly in the background, and many proprietary chatbots won’t show you their in-process “thinking” prompts even if you ask.

In the case of an AI poster, it might break down “make a poster” into smaller steps such as “create a design brief for a poster.” To demonstrate this while doing some testing for this piece, I added additional prompts for ChatGPT to explain the “design briefs” it generated, which included details like layout, colors, and typography.

In a recent development, the problem is those instructions are still subject to the same flaws as any other AI-generated text. They can’t properly fact-check; they can’t walk into the real world and see the thing they’re describing; and they can hallucinate or fall back on stale formats that become easy to notice after a while.

In a recent development, for example, while testing, I had ChatGPT generate a poster for a Lifehacker-themed nightclub. In every case, the underlying brief it generated outlined some basic details, but occasionally it added things I hadn’t asked for. This included additional text, iconography, and in one case it even added the “design brief” explanation I had requested as the bottom half of the poster.

In a recent development, those mistakes filter into the final product, when the brief is then fed into the image generator that ultimately makes the poster. In my case, ChatGPT showed me the underlying explanations for its reasoning (though even that could be different from what was actually sent to the image generator), but most people who use a chatbot for this task won’t see these factors before getting the final result.

In a recent development, while most chatbots won’t show you exactly what underlying “thinking” they use, most can be coaxed into describing the vague outlines of how they reached certain outcomes. And those descriptions provide some insight into why certain chatbots keep outputting similar results over and over. It doesn’t take long for some patterns to emerge. For example, any prompt to generate a poster for a nightclub almost invariably generated a brief that had specifications for a color palette including “electric purple,” “electric yellow,” and “electric pink.”.

It has been revealed that the reason for this should be pretty obvious: When the statistical model underlying LLMs needs to come up with an example for “colors for a nightclub poster,” the most obvious answers are neon, high-energy colors. Unless you know something about the specific club’s vibe (and write that out and feed it to the chatbot), the AI will have to fill in the gaps with something. And that something will be based on the same statistics it uses to predict any word.

This pattern of repetition was everywhere in all the design rationale ChatGPT gave me. Across multiple attempts to generate a Club Lifehacker poster, the generated design brief added an overarching “concept” that described the fictional club’s atmosphere as “high-energy” and “futuristic.” Every bot mentioned using images with the “silhouette” of either the DJ or a dancing crowd (often both). All the text had to be “bold” and “futuristic.".

Industry observers note that if there's one dead giveaway that a poster was made with AI, it's that one brush-stroke font that they all seem to use. Now, this is a bit more speculative, but I have a theory on where that specific design comes from. And it’s worth noting upfront that this seems to only apply to posters generated by ChatGPT specifically.

It has been revealed that one of the most common factors I found in my design brief testing was the use of phrases like “brush lettering” or “brush script.” Brush lettering is a design term that refers to using any number of methods like markers, paint brushes, or brush pens to write text. In digital design, that can take the form of fonts that are designed to emulate the look of fancy, handwritten text.

Industry observers note that in every test poster I created, however, ChatGPT seemed to take the phrase “brush lettering” rather literally. Every instance I encountered of a design brief that mentioned any kind of “brush” text generated an image with letters that looked as though they were created with a broad paint brush. A human designer would understand “brush lettering” to mean “something that looks handwritten," but ChatGPT didn’t seem capable of understanding the phrase as anything other than using an actual paint brush.

Sources indicate that the generated posters aren’t even using a “font,” strictly speaking. (Often, letters that should be identical had slight variations.) The image generator part of the chatbot is still a diffusion model, so it can’t employ a vector-based font, per se. But the brush-style font is so common that its look surfaces in any statistical model.

Sources indicate that this is an odd quirk of ChatGPT specifically, and it’s possible that it could change in the future. Especially if OpenAI intentionally tries to train this behavior out of its chatbot. However, it’s helpful to illustrate the underlying mechanism. The only way a chatbot can conceptualize design elements in a visual medium is to generate more specific text to feed to the image generator. And that text is just as prone to mistakes and blandness as any other AI model.

According to recent reports, I’ve been examining this with a focus on the kinds of posters ChatGPT generates because they’re very common, but posters (or any AI-generated content) from other models might look different. Every model has its own tendencies. For example, a lot of vibecoded websites are made with Anthropic’s Claude, and you can often tell by the tiny text, buttons with rounded corners, and tile-based layouts.

Recent findings suggest that to a certain extent, this is inevitable. While AI models are very different from humans and do not make “choices” in the same way people do, design elements still have to come from somewhere, and whether human or AI, it’s impossible to make these decisions in a vacuum. Humans will have preferences based on the things they like or emotionally resonate with, and AI models will have tendencies based on what their statistical model determines is the most appropriate output.

Recent findings suggest that that means that an AI model’s “style” is naturally going to change over time. Even if a model improves or makes fewer mistakes, it’s impossible to ever change the fact that all ChatGPT images are made by ChatGPT. Whatever you generate with any particular model will have a lot in common with what everyone else who uses the same tool generates.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • macOS 27.3 beta 2 adds a blue menu bar indicator for apps using System & App Protection Override.
  • If you regularly use trusted automation tools and utilities, that can mean a persistent pill taking up space in your menu bar.
  • I’ve tested this on macOS 27.3 beta 2 and confirmed that the indicator disappears after a restart.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

macOS 27.3 beta 2 adds a blue menu bar indicator for apps using System & App Protection Override. Apple describes itas a transparency indicator that appears when one app is controlling another.

If you regularly use trusted automation tools and utilities, that can mean a persistent pill taking up space in your menu bar. Prefer to hide it? There’s a Terminal workaround.

I’ve tested this on macOS 27.3 beta 2 and confirmed that the indicator disappears after a restart.

Open Terminal and run these two commands:.

sudo mkdir -p /Library/Preferences/FeatureFlags/Domainsudo defaults write /Library/Preferences/FeatureFlags/Domain/TCC AX_TRANSPARENCY_INDICATOR -dict Enabled -bool false.

Enter your Mac administrator password when prompted, then restart your Mac.

According to recent reports, the command disables the internal AX_TRANSPARENCY_INDICATOR feature flag. It doesn’t remove apps from your permissions list, although you’ll no longer see this activity indicator.

To restore Apple’s default behavior, run:.

sudo defaults delete /Library/Preferences/FeatureFlags/Domain/TCC AX_TRANSPARENCY_INDICATOR.

It has been revealed that restart your Mac again to apply the reversal. This removes only the indicator override, preserving any other flags you may have configured.

This is an undocumented workaround tested on the current beta, so Apple could change or remove it in a future revision.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This week's column is bleak. First, there's the looksmaxxing trend where teenagers are taking dangerous chemicals to correct perceived physical shortcomings. Then there are the AI job interviewers. Depressing, but at least some young people are having a little fun with their dystopian hellscape.

You can judge a generation by the illegal drugs it pioneers. In the 1960s, hippies smoked weed and dropped acid to expand their consciousness; the yuppies of the go-go '80s fueled their drive to acquire with Colombian cocaine; but kids today don’t want to go deeper or work harder. They have a smaller, sadder goal: They take drugs to look better. The substance of choice for a growing number of teenage boys are steroids, peptides, and other exotic chemicals designed to enhance appearance.

According to recent reports, would-be muscle-men have been injecting themselves with black market ‘rhoids since the Eisenhower administration, but that was a small cult of adult weirdos with a specific goal. In 2026, kids are into it, and they aren’t using steroids to win a $500 prize in the Mr. Topeka contest; they’re using unapproved research chemicals to looksmaxx. Looksmaxxing is an online movement of young men trying to maximize their physical appearance. Teenagers are taking the normal desire to look their best to dangerous, pathological levels. Driven by a combination of undiagnosed body dysmorphia and relentless social media algorithms that turn amoral “red pill” kooks into gurus, teenage boys are ingesting a panoply of exotic and dangerous compounds in a quest to fix the angle of their jawlines, change their skin tone, lose weight, grow taller, and otherwise “correct” perceived physical problems.

Recent findings suggest that in the "good old days" of steroid abuse, people generally stuck to abusing anabolic-androgenic steroids that had at least been tested for decades. Teens today are buying SARMs (Selective Androgen Receptor Modulators) and synthetic peptides marked "not for human consumption" from shady laboratories online. Steroids primarily affect the muscles, but many of these newer substances target different biological systems. A recent Rolling Stone article reports that kids are “heightmaxxing” by swallowing erdafitinib, a drug that treats advanced urothelial cancer, because the drug is known to trigger growth spurts (that can result in a curvature of the spine and other nasty side effects). They’re also trying MK-677 to get taller, an experimental growth hormone secretagogue that carries the risk of insulin resistance, water retention, and high blood pressure. Others are injecting Melanotan II, a synthetic peptide that forces a long-lasting deep tan, with side effects of extreme nausea and the sudden, aggressive darkening of moles. (And they're doing steroids too.).

It has been revealed that in the looksmaxxing community, softmaxxing is doing generally-considered-acceptable things to look better, like getting enough sleep, exercising regularly, and eating a balanced diet. Hardmaxxing is taking more extreme measures like plastic surgery, smashing your face with a hammer, or taking experimental drugs.

In the bodybuilding and looksmaxxing community, “natty” refers to a natural, non-steroid-enhanced physique.

In a recent development, here's something more lighthearted than the growing popularity of illicit self-esteem chemicals: the bicep heart and waist heart trends. The Bicep heart came first. Thirst trap videos started appearing on Instagram and TikTok in October in which dudes make a heart with their hand and bicep. Then people started posting variations where they frame the shot with someone they love inside the heart. The bicep heart swiftly led to women posting the waist heart.

Sources indicate that okay. So maybe it's not that lighthearted of a trend. While there are some videos of dudes with skinny arms doing the bicep heart, it's mostly jacked dudes. And the waist heart doesn't seem like it would work at all unless you are a specific shape, as this video illustrates. So maybe this isn't a silly meme but an illustration of how young people are inundated with content that can trigger feelings of physical unworthiness, even if they're just looking for silly memes.

It has been revealed that as if searching for a job wasn't alienating and horrible enough, some companies have begun using AI agents to conduct interviews. Begging a robot to let you work in a cubicle farm is as dystopian as anything Phillip K. Dick ever imagined, but don't count humanity out yet. Young people are sticking a finger in the eye of the machine by creating comedy videos that focus on trolling these AI job interviewers. They're hilarious because AI is the ultimate straight person in a comedy team, and the raw compute costs to run these interviews means corporate money is burning with each second of wasted time. Here are some of the top creators in the genre.

Bo Bongo: This YouTuber indicates up to AI interviews shirtless but insists he's wearing a "corporate tube top," then focuses on daring the interviewer to notice he's doing things like smoking a cigarette or eating a rotisserie chicken.

Cam Whitt likes to wind up AI by arguing, interrupting, telling outrageous lies, and asking the dumbest questions imaginable, like, "When does the interview actually start?" and "How do I figure out what my name is?".

Grahamn Raabe: Among this YouTuber's schticks is speaking only in nonsense, like describing his professional background as "freight cadence, walnut, a little bit of Richard, spruce wood—six years of spruce wood.".

Nick Reid: Is so obnoxious, he seems to make the AI furious at him, even though it's a computer without emotions. Two thumbs up!

💡 Key Takeaways
  • DC just shared a newly introduced image of its latest iteration of Robin, answering a major fan question about this new hero's superpowers.
  • DC recently rebooted the iconic Legion of Super-Heroes - a group of superhumans from the 31st Century, inspired to found a fresh 'Age of Heroes' by the legacy of the modern day Superman.
  • According to recent reports, DC recently unveiled the latest recruit to the Legion would be Bat-Lad - a future version of Robin who follows Batman's legacy rather than the Man of Steel's.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

DC just shared a newly introduced image of its latest iteration of Robin, answering a major fan question about this new hero's superpowers. Here's the new art, and everything we know about the latest Boy Wonder.

DC recently rebooted the iconic Legion of Super-Heroes - a group of superhumans from the 31st Century, inspired to found a fresh 'Age of Heroes' by the legacy of the modern day Superman. With Brainiac hunting different versions of the Legion across the multiverse, they find themselves beset by an enemy they can't comprehend.

According to recent reports, DC recently unveiled the latest recruit to the Legion would be Bat-Lad - a future version of Robin who follows Batman's legacy rather than the Man of Steel's. The first art of the character raised questions about his powers that DC has just answered.

Industry observers note that DC recently revealed V. Ken Marion's cover for Legion of Super-Heroes #4, showing Bat-Lad in action. The young hero is shown in a dingy street with a shadowy being behind him. This is something fans already saw in Hayden Sherman and Tamra Bonvillain's main cover (below), but it far more clearly communicates the newly introduced hero's powers.

While that cover revealed a silhouette behind Bat-Lad, Marion's art makes it clear that the shadow is a physical being controlled by Bat-Lad, with its Venom-like ichor curling around his arm. It's also clear that the original cover isn't obscuring this shadow being - the all-black appearance is its official design.

Recent findings suggest that the new cover appears to confirm that Bat-Lad is essentially a reverse-Robin. While the original Robin is Batman's sidekick, Bat-Lad appears to be able to summon a towering creature of living darkness. It's an awesome twist on the 'Batman and Robin' partnership, showing how Batman's legacy has been warped over the centuries.

Sadly, it seems that Bat-Lad's powers have a major drawback, as the summary for the issue tells fans to "Welcome a boy and his uncontrollable shadow monster to the world of Legion!" Despite this, DC refers to Bat-Lad as a "newly introduced legionnaire," confirming he'll join the team.

It has been revealed that fans don't yet know much about Bat-Lad other than that he dresses in Robin's colors and can summon a shadow monster. However, it's possible he comes from Planet Gotham. This location was introduced in 2020's Legion of Super-Heroes, characterized as the galaxy's first artificially created planet.

Planet Gotham echoes Batman's iconic city, with a noir aesthetic and ruled over by a president referred to as the 'Commissioner.' The populace are served by robots using the holographic visage of Bruce Wayne's butler Alfred Pennyworth and policed by androids in the style of Victorian 'bobbies.'.

Planet Gotham is characterized as an essentially crime-free utopia, but one with a strict rule of law. Casinos and gaudy luxury are everywhere, suggesting the limits of Batman's ability to truly change Gotham's spirit, no matter the time frame.

Sources indicate that DC's 31st Century was canonically rewritten by recent events, so the world of the Legion of Super-Heroes isn't quite as fans remember it. That could mean that Planet Gotham no longer exists, however with each Legionnaire tending to be from a different planet, so it would make a lot of sense for Bat-Lad to call Planet Gotham home.

The Legion of Super-Heroes are known for having a massive membership, making even the Justice League at its height look small. Each era adds a few fresh heroes, often as commentary on DC lore at the time or on modern-day themes.

It has been revealed that the last major addition to the team was the mysterious Gold Lantern, who became an object of fascination for fans and built on the idea of the multi-colored Lantern Corps. Now, the Robin of the 3st Century is set to join the team, as Bat-Lad heads towards his debut.

Legion of Super-Heroes #4 is coming December 9 from DC Comics.

#16868. 6 Western Movies From the ’90s That Are 10/10 Masterpieces

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1397 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Collider ↗ Open Full Page

6 Western Movies From the ’90s That Are 10/10 Masterpieces

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1397 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Collider

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • There's nothing quite like a good Western.
  • Whether you prefer comedic takes on the genre, action-packed shoot-'em-ups, or deconstructive takes that raise the Western from the ground up, there's something here for everyone.
  • In a recent development, starting this list off with perhaps the most controversial pick, Young Guns II deserves its place in the Western canon.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There's nothing quite like a good Western. Although the golden age of the horse opera was undoubtedly the mid-20th century, the genre continued to persevere long afterward. In fact, there was a Western renaissance in the 1990s that took Hollywood — and the Academy Awards — by storm. From genre staples like Clint Eastwood and Kevin Costner to visionary filmmakers like Ang Lee and Richard Donner, the '90s sparked new life into the Old West.

Whether you prefer comedic takes on the genre, action-packed shoot-'em-ups, or deconstructive takes that raise the Western from the ground up, there's something here for everyone. Outlaws, lawmen, soldiers, and cowboys galore make up some of the greatest thrills of the '90s centered entirely on the American West. Whether you adore these flicks already or have yet to visit them, these are some of the decade's greatest Westerns — so don't sleep on them.

In a recent development, starting this list off with perhaps the most controversial pick, Young Guns II deserves its place in the Western canon. A high-octane sequel to the original 1988 flick, the Emilio Estevez-led Billy the Kid action romp pits the Regulators against the lawman Pat Garrett (William Petersen), who aims to bring Billy and his friends in on several outstanding warrants. The result is an intense cat-and-mouse ride across the Upcoming Mexican desert, and it's a blast for those who haven't had the pleasure.

Sources indicate that young Guns II is arguably even greater than its predecessor. Billy, Doc (Kiefer Sutherland), Chavez (Lou Diamond Phillips), and the rest of the Regulators carry the weight of the picture with their trademark charm and "Brat Pack" pull. The fast-pulling sequel does everything it can to surpass the original, armed with a killer Jon Bon Jovi theme and plenty of fabulous performances that deserve high praise. There's a reason that folks are still calling for a third entry after all these years — and long after the fates of the Regulators have already been met.

According to recent reports, the Wild West era and the American Civil War are so inexplicably linked that one cannot divorce the Western from the war itself. Director Ang Lee understood this profoundly when tackling Ride with the Devil, a Civil War-era trial by fire that chronicles a group of Missouri Bushwhackers as they battle the Jayhawkers invading their Southern home. Its meditations on the origins of Western violence as an outgrowth from the war itself are quite complex, and the picture pulls no punches as it does so. Tobey Maguire and Skeet Ulrich star as childhood friends Jake Roedel and Jack Bull Chiles seek revenge on those who threatened their home.

Recent findings suggest that like many Westerns, Ride with the Devil offers a nuanced take on the war that explores the evils of both sides. That noted, the Irregulars are portrayed as almost akin to a typical Western outlaw gang. Jake's struggle with the Southern cause, and his growing friendship with former slave Daniel Holt (Jeffrey Wright), is what forges his path as an honorable man. It may not be the first film that comes to mind when you think of the Old West — indeed it's very much rooted in the Civil War itself — but it would be hard to consider the film anything but a Western in style and substance.

Recent findings suggest that based on the popular Western television program of the same name, Richard Donnor brought Bret Maverick (Mel Gibson) to the major screen with the comedic Maverick. When the titular gambler finds himself in search of the funds to enter a high-stakes poker game, he ventures across the Old West alongside Annabelle Bransford (Jodie Foster) and Marshal Zane Cooper (James Garner), who certainly give him a run for his money. If you loved the show, you'll get a kick out of the big-screen version.

Industry observers note that maverick reminds us, like Young Guns II, that the genre can be fun as much as it is introspective. Gibson plays the unusual Western "hero" with genuine charm and an unassuming con artistry that certainly honors the original series. It's not your typical Western, but that's exactly why it's such a stellar entry. Of course, Maverick turns out to actually be a continuation rather than a straight-up reboot, but the way it reveals such a fact is exactly the sort of slight-of-hand that gives Bret Maverick his edge.

Four icons and four completely different ways of walking into trouble. This is the one you would have been out there, why it fits, and what it would have cost you.

You have never explained yourself and you have never needed to, because people work out fairly quickly that you are the most capable person in the room without you ever having to mention it.

You are the funniest person in most rooms and the most loyal person in all of them, and you would be genuinely insulted if somebody suggested those two things were in any tension.

You never wanted this job, and you took it anyway because the alternative was standing there watching somebody less careful do it badly, which is the most Western reason there has ever been.

Nobody has ever successfully talked you out of something you had already decided was right, and a long line of grown adults has found that out the hard way.

In a recent development, the first Western to win Best Picture at the Oscars in decades, Dances with Wolves was Kevin Costner's directorial debut that proved the Western could be as epic as ever. With a screenplay by Michael Blake based on his novel of the same name, the film follows Lt. John Dunbar as he is stationed out on the American frontier following his heroic (but secretly suicidal) actions during the Civil War. Caught between the Pawnee and Sioux, Dunbar eventually finds himself on the other end of his own country's barrel.

Dances with Wolves is a breathtaking motion picture. It's an introspective glimpse into both the effects of the Civil War and the lives of the Native American peoples who lived on the frontier long before it was settled. More than that, it was a trailblazer in native representation in Hollywood, and though not a true story, is largely based on historical truths. Beyond that, it's also just a great time, as Costner proves himself to be one of the genre's biggest champions.

According to recent reports, is there a more well-known or highly-celebrated '90s Western by audiences and critics alike than Tombstone? The spectacular Kurt Russell-led picture follows former lawman Wyatt Earp, his two brothers, and their friend Doc Holliday (Val Kilmer) as they arrive in the titular Arizona town just in time to square off with the ravenous Cowboys gang. As they do, things go from bad to worse as Tombstone falls into chaos — and the Earps bring hell on their adversaries.

Tombstone does absolutely everything right. It's thrilling, action-packed, and chock-full of some of the best on-screen dialogue in the business. Russell and Kilmer steal the show, but the entire stacked cast more than prove themselves over the course of these fast-moving 130 minutes. It's hard to rank the best performances in Tombstone given how stellar each actor truly is, but we all know that this movie wouldn't work nearly as well without Val Kilmer.

According to recent reports, just two years after Dances with Wolves reminded everyone that the Western still had real life left in it, Unforgiven came in and nabbed that Best Picture Oscar for itself. Directed by Clint Eastwood, the genre star tackles his final on-screen Western as William Munny, an aged former gunslinger who returns for one last job to provide for his family. It's a stellar revisionist picture that does everything right as Eastwood bids the genre that made him a final heartfelt farewell.

It has been revealed that it doesn't get much better than Unforgiven. With brilliant performances by Morgan Freeman, Richard Harris, and Gene Hackman, the picture excels in the way it unpacks the genre's most famous tropes and reconstructs them into Eastwood's final dissertation on what makes the Western truly exceptional. There are few Westerns so highly celebrated as Unforgiven, and although Eastwood may best be known for his work on the Dollars Trilogy, there's a reason this won Best Picture.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Jensen Huang’s resignation as Nvidia CEO shook up the AI market and US economy last week, but now via The Wall Street Journal Huang has spoken out publicly for the first time since stepping down, and he signals he’s ready to return as CEO if asked.

Today Robbie Whelan at The Wall Street Journal published Jensen Huang’s first public statement since departing Nvidia last week.

“Since my departure, I’ve seen an outpouring of calls from Nvidia’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO,” Huang said in a short statement. “If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the organization, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.”.

To be clear, I’m also willing to step in as CEO of Nvidia if asked. I’ve owned several generations of their graphics cards, so I have plenty of experience with their products. More importantly, this is probably my best chance of finally having enough cash to afford a Mac with 32GB of RAM.

The timing is likely no coincidence, as Nvidia is set to report its quarterly earnings later today.

Even though Huang technically resigned as CEO rather than being fired, it was clear that his ouster wasn’t exactly his choice. Thus, today’s statement is the former CEO formally putting it out into the world that he’s ready to return if asked.

It has been revealed that since Huang stepped down, President Trump publicly called on Apple’s Tim Cook to step in as Nvidia CEO. But it’s expected that a newly introduced CEO—assuming it’s not Huang—will take much longer for the company to find and Cook is unlikely to want the job.

AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Tomsguide ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Nvidia bug is killing SSDs — is it “AI code incompetence,” customers ask?

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (622 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomsguide

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If you haven't updated your Nvidia drivers recently, you may want to hold off.
  • The bug was found in the two most recent Nvidia GPU driver updates — specifically 621.14 and 621.24 — for the Nvidia GeForce Game Ready Driver.
  • Industry observers note that the bug was discovered by TroubleGrid who reported that the bug causes the NVDisplay.Container.exe to write (save data) far too much information to an Nvidia log file that can degrade the SSD.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you haven't updated your Nvidia drivers recently, you may want to hold off. A newly discovered bug apparently can damage your PC by writing excessive amounts of data to solid-state drives (SSDs).

The bug was found in the two most recent Nvidia GPU driver updates — specifically 621.14 and 621.24 — for the Nvidia GeForce Game Ready Driver. The 621.24 update was released on November 12.

Industry observers note that the bug was discovered by TroubleGrid who reported that the bug causes the NVDisplay.Container.exe to write (save data) far too much information to an Nvidia log file that can degrade the SSD. It can result in as much as 30GB per hour.

The executable already wrote log files before the updates but not that much. SSDs typically take years to degrade, but the excessive data written by this bug can speed up the process causing stuttering and mouse lag.

It has been revealed that on Reddit, I've seen a few posts about the bug with users complaining that this is why you never upgrade. "By principle I never ever update my drivers unless there are feature inclusions for let's say a latest game I bought," one Redditor noted.

Plenty of others agreed with that sentiment, and I'm inclined to say they're correct here.

The other half of the comments split between blaming AI-written code. Before his ouster, CEO Jensen Huang was pushing for Nvidia engineers to use more AI-generated code via chatbots and agents.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

According to recent reports, or they were of the belief that Nvidia is purposely killing drives to force customers to pay more for latest ones. Several called out Sam Altman and his recent claim that laptop RAM is a "terrible" allocation of a scarce resource.

"I honestly would not be surprised if they are doing this on purpose to kill our NVMe's," wrote a poster.

If we were to put blame on something, at this point, I'd say its AI-fueled incompetence, not AI-fueled greed, though that has led to mentioned stupidity.

The easiest fix is to rollback your graphics card driver to version 621.01, which is the last known patch to lack this bug.

Sources indicate that troubleGrid listed a manual fix that requires you to set the Nvidia Display Container LS service to manual. Though it'll cost you. Basically, this can disable the Nvidia Control Panel and Nvidia App, meaning G-Sync color settings, display scaling, resolution overrides and more will not rock. "Do not disable the service outright if you use G-SYNC or a custom colour profile," the report warns.

According to recent reports, if you need a temporary fix, you can stop the service, delete the log file and start again. However, the file will return and continue to grow in size.

Sources indicate that and if you'd prefer a more traditional freestanding barbecue setup, the Q2200N is also compatible with Weber's portable BBQ cart, which raises it to a more comfortable cooking height. It's sold separately, but the wheeled, foldable design makes it a handy addition for smaller outdoor spaces.

Recent findings suggest that if you're looking for a quality barbecue that won't dominate your balcony, courtyard or patio, the Weber Q2200N is a compelling option. #16857. Industry News: There's Actually a Simple Explanation for All These Widespread Outages

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (883 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Lifehacker ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: There's Actually a Simple Explanation for All These Widespread Outages

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (883 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It feels like every time you look at your phone lately, another firm is having an outage.
  • Industry observers note that that pattern, in turn, has begun to fuel anxiety among the general public.
  • government, these trickles of information aren't necessarily reassuring.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It feels like every time you look at your phone lately, another firm is having an outage. Last week, there was Microsoft, whose outage took down services from Outlook to Teams. Then, the FAA grounded all flights across the U.S. following "communication issues." This week, a number of banks experienced outages, as did Apple. Even the NSA's internal communications network went dark. Some of the biggest corporations and organizations in the world can't seem to keep their services running, leading to widespread disruptions and confusion. When it's a one-off, it's an annoyance; when it's outage after outage, it starts to feel like a pattern.

Industry observers note that that pattern, in turn, has begun to fuel anxiety among the general public. What could possibly be causing Apple, Microsoft, JP Morgan Chase, and the NSA alike to go dark at roughly the same time? Is it a coordinated cyberattack? An AI revolt? Is the end finally nigh? To an outside observer, it certainly appears like something coordinated and nefarious is happening here. Secretary of State Marco Rubio is insistent that there is "zero evidence" that hackers or bad actors caused any of these outages, and President Trump is particularly unconcerned by the whole ordeal, saying, "It's life," and "Things like that happen.".

But to skeptics of the U.S. government, these trickles of information aren't necessarily reassuring. While I agree with calls for someone from the government (perhaps the president himself) to make an official announcement explaining the situation, the root cause does appear to be clear at this time: The short answer? AI is at fault here, but not in the way you think.

Sources indicate that love it or hate it, AI is a force to be reckoned with. While you might know that AI can generate hyper-realistic videos and manage your emails on your behalf, certain models are adept at discovering newly introduced security vulnerabilities in software. These models aren't just helpful tools; they far surpass the abilities of human researchers. You might remember Anthropic initially pulled the brakes on its breakthrough model, Claude Mythos, when it found that the model could root out security vulnerabilities in just about anything.

Industry observers note that mythos, and models like it, are a double-edged sword. On the one hand, they can be major assets for developers and researchers to find new security vulnerabilities that humans otherwise wouldn't have discovered, and patch them accordingly. Unfortunately, the same can be noted for bad actors, who can use these models to learn about new security flaws and attempt to exploit them before researchers have a chance to find them. As such, software developers across the spectrum, from small-time devs to major corporations, have been racing to patch as many security vulnerabilities as they can find—and they're finding a lot.

It has been revealed that you might notice your PC's security updates, for example, are shipping with more patches than usual—historic levels, even. Microsoft keeps breaking its own records with its Patch Tuesday updates, including over 1,400 fixes with its October patch. The company's October 2025 Patch Tuesday update, by comparison, included fewer than 180 fixes.

It's notable to understand that just about every tech giant that develops software is furiously working to patch its systems before hackers or AI agents exploit vulnerabilities first. And while there are successes (Microsoft is now protecting its customers from thousands of flaws each month), this speed is also inadvertently breaking things along the way. That's not just speculation: According to The Washington Sun, both Wall Street executives and the NSA explained to members of Congress that patching security flaws discovered by AI models caused this week's widespread outages.

Barring some campaign to cover up a coordinated attack on systems and services, it does seem like these outages are simply the result of companies breaking their own products in an attempt to stop AI-assisted hackers from exploiting undiscovered flaws. But that's not all that reassuring, either. AI models are only going to keep getting better at finding vulnerabilities; likewise, AI agents are only improving at hacking into systems autonomously. Companies will need to ramp up their efforts to patch their software before both hackers and AI agents discover those flaws first, and so the cycle will continue. Unless something changes, we may see routine outages as companies try to fix things as rapidly as possible.

The implications aren't specific to any one tech giant, either. Our world increasingly relies on fewer companies to keep us all connected. We saw that last year, when cloud hosting providers like AWS and Cloudflare each experienced outages. When these services go down, so do all of the networks that rely on them. If AWS or Cloudflare break something while trying to patch their systems, whole parts of the internet go dark.

Sources indicate that of course, it'll only be more difficult for the general public—if not the developers themselves—to recognize when outages are the result of maintenance or a cyberattack. Just because recent outages don't appear to be nefarious in nature, that doesn't mean future outages will be so innocent. For the time being, however, it seems we can worry less about an active cybersecurity incident, and more about how AI is disrupting modern life in ways few of us saw coming.

#16851. 'Yellowjackets' season 4 review: A strong start but too many unanswered questions risk a 'Lost'-style ending

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (805 w)

'Yellowjackets' season 4 review: A strong start but too many unanswered questions risk a 'Lost'-style ending

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (805 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomsguide

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • For five years and three seasons, Paramount’s “Yellowjackets” has been at once enthralling and appalling audiences.
  • According to recent reports, what eventually roped me in and made it impossible to look away were the stellar performances from the massive ensemble cast and the storytelling that — cliché as it sounds — actually left me on the edge of my seat, peeking out in horror from behind my fingers.
  • Heading into the show’s fourth and final season, though, those strengths become double-edged swords.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For five years and three seasons, Paramount’s “Yellowjackets” has been at once enthralling and appalling audiences. As someone who is easily squeamish, I’ll admit that when I first tuned in years ago, I almost abandoned the show altogether, too disturbed by watching teenagers hunt their friends like animals and decapitate corpses to continue.

According to recent reports, what eventually roped me in and made it impossible to look away were the stellar performances from the massive ensemble cast and the storytelling that — cliché as it sounds — actually left me on the edge of my seat, peeking out in horror from behind my fingers. Adding to that was “Yellowjackets’” knack for unveiling mysteries that left viewers, myself included, desperate for answers.

Heading into the show’s fourth and final season, though, those strengths become double-edged swords. The major questions that kept audiences hooked for years now demand answers before the series finale. Likewise, the interwoven narrative — jumping between the teenage plane crash survivors stranded in the wilderness and their adult counterparts — has always been an effective tool, but before the end, these timelines need to find a satisfying cohesion.

Having watched the first eight of season 4's 10 episodes, I can safely and somewhat unfortunately say that while “Yellowjackets” satisfies in some areas, it falls short in others — and it doesn’t have much time left to course-correct.

Easily the most compelling aspect of these first eight episodes is the exploration of the team’s return home. For three seasons, audiences knew these traumatized kids — the ones who survived, at least — would eventually make it back, with the adult timeline confirming several names (Shauna, Misty, and Melissa among them).

Prior to season 4, however, “Yellowjackets” had yet to reveal that exact moment of return and its immediate fallout: watching characters who hunted, killed, and ate their friends attempt to slip back into their “normal” lives. While the adult timeline already proved the survivors never truly moved past their ordeal, seeing their parent reunions, the jarring shift in high school social dynamics, and the strange fame that comes with surviving a mass tragedy is precisely what audiences have been waiting for.

It has been revealed that with just two episodes to go, a shocking number of questions remain on the table, raising an obvious concern: has “Yellowjackets” saved too much for an epic finale? Of the many indicates met with controversy over their endings, the mind-bending sci-fi series “Lost” is among the most notorious and perhaps the closest comparison to “Yellowjackets” in its approach to mystery and suspense.

Sources indicate that like “Lost,” “Yellowjackets” has spent years building complex mysteries whose reveals appear to be crammed into the final two episodes. In the case of “Lost,” that famously backfired, leaving even dedicated fans frustrated by how questions were answered, the breakneck speed with which some were “resolved,” or the fact that certain mysteries went unaddressed forever.

Recent findings suggest that based on episodes 1 through 8, “Yellowjackets” season 4 seems to be heading down a very similar path. Several of the show’s most captivating questions haven't just gone unanswered by the end of episode 8, they’ve been largely ignored. Hopefully, this doesn't mean answers are never coming, which would undoubtedly trigger a wave of backlash akin to “Lost.” Even if the finale delivers, it would have been far more satisfying to see this final season deeply flesh out the truth of the wilderness — whether it’s a supernatural force or simply a manifestation of the survivors’ trauma — well before the final curtain.

Sources indicate that ultimately, “Yellowjackets” Season 4 is an exciting final entry that showcases the cast at the top of their game and finally gives audiences a real look at how the survivors reacclimated—or failed to—after nearly two years in the wild. Still, for the final chapter of a show that has captivated viewers for five years, the series has left itself too much ground to cover in too little time.

According to recent reports, while heavy narrative exposition was always inevitable in Season 4—especially with so much left unresolved in the adult timeline—what audiences really want heading into the finale are answers, not more questions. With the clock very much ticking, “Yellowjackets” still has to prove it can stick the landing.

"Yellowjackets" season 4 episode 1 is streaming now on Paramount+.

  • Professional and amateur photographers just got a new alternative for editing and managing their photos on Mac with the release of VSCO Studio Pro, a native macOS app that brings the company’s popular editing tools to the desktop for the first time.
  • More than that, VSCO Studio Pro integrates with the company’s broader ecosystem of photography tools, allowing customers to manage their workflow from importing and editing photos to delivering finished images to clients through VSCO Galleries, without having to manually export and upload them to another app.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

VSCO today released Studio Pro Desktop, its first native photo editor for Mac, bringing many of the company’s familiar editing tools to macOS, alongside new features aimed at photographers working with large numbers of images. Here are the details.

Professional and amateur photographers just got a new alternative for editing and managing their photos on Mac with the release of VSCO Studio Pro, a native macOS app that brings the company’s popular editing tools to the desktop for the first time.

More than that, VSCO Studio Pro integrates with the company’s broader ecosystem of photography tools, allowing customers to manage their workflow from importing and editing photos to delivering finished images to clients through VSCO Galleries, without having to manually export and upload them to another app.

It also supports keyboard shortcuts similar to those found in other popular photo editors, making it easier for photographers familiar with those apps to get started.

Here’s Eric Wittman, CEO of VSCO, on today’s launch:.

Sources indicate that “Photographers deserve tools built around how they actually work. […] 75% of VSCO Pro members have used our presets in the last six months. Now those looks live on the desktop, with one connected workflow from camera to client delivery and nothing getting in the way.

In a recent development, the first thing users will notice, and then continue to notice when using VSCO Studio Pro, is how fast it is. From changing the grid size, to sorting images, to applying presets by rolling the cursor over each of the 200+ presets, pretty much everything about VSCO Studio Pro feels as real-time and instant as it can be when dealing with large numbers of images.

As for importing photos, VSCO Studio Pro supports Apple Photos, local folders, SD cards, and external drives, and offers RAW compatibility with more than 800 cameras from 20 brands. Customers can also choose whether to work with files in their original location or copy them elsewhere.

Under the hood, VSCO Studio Pro Desktop combines Apple’s Core Image RAW processing with the manufacturer’s own Reflex image processing engine, which handles presets and editing adjustments.

Batch editing in VSCO Studio Pro Desktop can handle anywhere from two to 500 images at once, which is great for quickly applying the same preset or film-inspired look (including Kodak Portra, Kodachrome, Fujifilm Velvia, and Kodak Tri-X), or making adjustments to an entire set of photos simultaneously, with changes appearing across all selected images in real time.

According to recent reports, and speaking of presets, VSCO Studio Pro packs an exclusive one called IOE1 Pro, developed with photographer Joe Greer. IOE1 Pro, as well as VSCO’s other presets, allow users to adjust the strength, color, tone, and contrast, further helping them fine-tune each look to their liking.

VSCO Studio Pro’s editing tools include the usual suspects photographers might expect from photo editing software, including exposure, contrast, fade, highlights, shadows, whites, blacks, skin tone, temperature, tint, hue, saturation, lightness, sharpening, clarity, vignetting, and grain adjustments for strength, size, and color.

VSCO is also working to expand its toolset to include bloom and halation effects, curves, masks, and a remove tool for users looking for more control over their edits and to make more precise, localized adjustments to their images.

Also in the works are fresh organizational features, including projects for managing groups of photos, as well as culling tools that will allow users to rate images with stars and mark them as accepted or rejected, making it easier to sort through large photo collections.

Once people are happy with their adjustments, they can export their photos individually or in batches, choosing the file name, format, resolution, and compression quality. VSCO Studio Pro also offers resizing presets for web, social media, and client delivery, as well as the option to save the finished images to a folder of their choice.

And speaking of client delivery, consumers can publish their edited photos directly to VSCO Galleries, allowing them to share full-resolution images without having to export them and upload them separately elsewhere.

VSCO Studio Pro Desktop is available today as a free download for Apple Silicon Macs, with full feature access requiring a VSCO Pro membership, starting at $4.99 per month or $59.99 per year, or a VSCO One membership. You can see it in action below:.

Amid accusations of antisemitism over a recent episode of Las Culturistas, Bowen Yang has issued an apology.

On Friday, the 5x Emmy nominee released a statement explaining he was unaware of the “antisemitic history” of the word “Zio,” which he recently used in reference to Regina Spektor removing a pro-Palestine protester from her concert.

“I want to genuinely apologize for using a word on the podcast without knowing its antisemitic history, especially since we’ve repudiated antisemitism on the show as recently as the last two weeks,” he wrote in the statement on Instagram. “Particularly upsetting to realize that I adopted language popularized by far-right movements whose rhetoric we should be wary of and act against.”.

Yang added on his Instagram Story, “At the same time, Free Palestine.” Watch on Deadline.

Although some thought Yang’s apology wasn’t enough, many in the comments have called out the criticism for being in bad faith, with the common assumption that the term is short for “Zionism,” which originated in the 19th century as a movement to establish a Jewish homeland.

But the ADL considers it to be an “antisemitic slur popularized by notorious white supremacist leader and former KKK Grand Wizard David Duke,” with ADL CEO Jonathan Greenblatt accusing Yang of providing “a textbook example of normalizing antisemitism.”.

Industry observers note that “Seriously? Apologizing for your antisemitism with not one, but two qualifications isn’t an apology at all,” wrote Greenblatt in part. “It was a reminder that you don’t feel like Jews deserve the same respect as everyone else. That’s not political speech; it’s prejudice — and it’s pathetic.”.

Despite accusations of antisemitism, Yang and Las Culturistas co-host Matt Rogers have called out Zionism on multiple occasions as it pertains to the occupation of Gaza.

According to recent reports, since Israel’s ongoing strikes on Gaza in the wake of Hamas’ Oct. 7, 2023 attack, multiple organizations have classified Israel’s actions as a genocide against Palestinians, including the United Nations, Amnesty International and Human Rights Watch.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Most of the conversation around iOS 27 was centered on Apple’s upgraded, AI-powered Siri, which brings deeper on-screen awareness and smarter multi-step actions.
  • If you have been putting off the upgrade assuming there is nothing in it for older hardware, it is worth reconsidering.
  • In a recent development, scammers frequently rely on high-pressure calls and spoofed texts to trick you into wiring funds or surrendering credentials.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Most of the conversation around iOS 27 was centered on Apple’s upgraded, AI-powered Siri, which brings deeper on-screen awareness and smarter multi-step actions. The catch is that Apple Intelligence requires an iPhone 15 Pro or newer, leaving anyone holding onto an older compatible handset locked out of the headline feature.

If you have been putting off the upgrade assuming there is nothing in it for older hardware, it is worth reconsidering. Beneath the AI marketing, Apple rolled out several high-impact security, camera, and interface upgrades that run without Apple Intelligence — and these three additions make a meaningful difference in daily use.

In a recent development, scammers frequently rely on high-pressure calls and spoofed texts to trick you into wiring funds or surrendering credentials. Introduced in iOS 27, Impersonation Risk Detection serves as Apple’s built-in defense against this social engineering, and it works without requiring Apple Intelligence.

To activate it, open Settings, tap Privacy & Security, scroll down and select Impersonation Risk Detection, then toggle it on.

The system monitors on-device interaction patterns and behavioral cues during high-stakes actions without reading your personal messages, emails, or photos. If you attempt a large transfer or sensitive account change under signs of coercion, your iPhone flags the event and directs supported banking apps to require secondary verification before funds can leave your account.

Sources indicate that over the last few iOS updates, Apple has tucked more manual toggles behind the Camera app’s six-dot menu, adding extra taps whenever you want to tweak exposure, aspect ratio, or timer settings before taking a shot. iOS 27 fixes that friction by letting you pin your essential controls directly to the top of the viewfinder.

Sources indicate that launch the Camera app, tap the six-dot icon and hit Edit in the top-left corner. From there, tap any highlighted tools you want kept within thumb’s reach, remove shortcuts you rarely touch using the minus badge, and tap Done.

Even better, iOS 27 saves separate pinned layouts per shooting mode, allowing you to tailor your quick-access toolbar individually for Photo, Portrait, Video, Cinematic, Slow-Mo, and Time-Lapse.

Industry observers note that apple’s translucent Liquid Glass design has remained one of iOS’s most polarizing visual shifts since its debut, particularly when semi-transparent menus sit over bright or busy wallpapers. Rather than forcing a one-size-fits-all look, iOS 27 introduces a dedicated precision slider so you can tailor how much transparency appears across your system interface.

Open Settings, tap Appearance, and select Liquid Glass to find the new control. Sliding the toggle to the left preserves the full see-through glass aesthetic, while moving it to the right applies a heavier, tinted backdrop that makes buttons and text significantly easier to read at a glance.

A live preview window sits directly above the slider so you can test the contrast before locking in your preferred look.

According to recent reports, as confirmed via premierleague.com, Sam Barrott will take charge of the match, with Adam Nunn and Lee Betts as his assistants, while Chris Kavanagh is fourth official. John Brooks is on VAR, assisted by Paul Howard.

The upcoming game is the Reds’ sixth home match in the top flight this season, and it’ll be the third to have had the Yorkshire native as the referee.

Upon learning that curious fact, Keith Hackett took to social media to endorse Barrott as a referee but question the decision-making process which has led to him being dispatched to Anfield once again.

The former chief executive of the PGMOL (now Pro Ref) posted on X: ‘A top-class referee, but not a very good appointing procedure by his bosses’.

Want more Empire of the Kop coverage? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for news you can trust.

It’s a strong show of faith by Pro Ref chief executive Howard Webb to assign Barrott to what is always the most high-profile fixture in English football, and arguably world football.

Liverpool fans might be forgiven for not being able to summon much enthusiasm over the appointment, given the official’s previous at Anfield this season.

In August, it was he who awarded Nottingham Forest a penalty in their 2-2 draw against the Reds when Neco Williams went to ground under a challenge from Alisson Becker. The Premier League’s Key Match Incidents Panel subsequently adjudged that the spot kick was wrongly given.

While there are clear critera which must be observed when appointing match officials to specific fixtures – any officials from Merseyside or Manchester are obviously ineligible for Sunday’s clash at Anfield – seeing Barrott assigned to yet another Liverpool home game does seem anomalous.

We just hope – for his sake as much as anyone else’s – that the main talking point after the final whistle isn’t a controversial and decisive error on his part. The last thing we need is yet more dubious refereeeing affecting the Reds.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that as temperatures drop, our lawns often show signs of wear and tear from battling the elements. Whether dealing with patchy growth, damaged areas, or waterlogged soil, we still need to give our yards extra lawn care for the harsh winter months ahead.

According to recent reports, perhaps one of the most crucial gardening tasks for healthy lawn growth is applying fertilizer. However, given the cooler conditions, is it too late to fertilize my lawn before winter?

To answer my question, I called on the gardening experts to answer this question — and offer their top tips and tricks. So before you prep your lawn fertilizer, here’s what you need to know.

According to experts, you can fertilize your lawn before winter — as long as it’s completed by mid-November at the latest.

“If you are looking to fertilize your lawn before winter, I would recommend you do this no later than the middle of November, as your grass is becoming dormant and growth is slowing around this time, so it is best to fertilize beforehand,” advises Craig Wilson, co-founder and gardening expert at Gardeners Dream.

While fertilizing is commonly associated with warmer weather, cold-weather lawn care relies on specialized formulas.

“Make sure to use a low-nitrogen fertiliser that features high-potassium levels, as this will help to protect your lawn better in the cold weather,” adds Wilson.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Fall fertilization supports stronger root systems, thicker turf, and lends better resistance to harsh conditions throughout the winter months.

Furthermore, choose a fertilizer designed to specifically help your lawn withstand and handle colder weather conditions.

“Fall fertilization supports stronger root systems, thicker turf, and lends better resistance to harsh conditions throughout the winter months,” states Brian Feldman, Senior Director of Operations and Agronomy at TruGreen.

“Make sure to select a fertilizer that’s formulated specifically for fall and apply it about 3-4 weeks before your area’s first expected frost, and while soil temperatures are still above 50 degrees F.”.

Of course, prepping your lawn for winter requires a few extra steps, including clearing away weeds, clearing fallen leaves, and debris to stop them from smothering the soil underneath.

“I would also advise continuing to keep your lawn clear of fallen leaves to avoid any dead patches of grass,” agrees Wilson.

“They needn’t go to waste though — you can spread them over your borders as a nutritious mulch for your plants, which will help improve the soil quality!”.

It has been revealed that while adding excess fertilizer seems like a good way to protect your lawn through the winter, it can actually do more harm than good. Avoid over-fertilizing if you don’t want to damage your lawn.

“Be careful not to over-fertilize, as too much can lead to nutrient runoff and weak, fast-growing grass that’s more prone to damage. The goal is strong, sustained growth from the roots up,” adds Feldman.

Other top tips include aerating your lawn and knowing when to plant grass seed in November.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Liverpool are ready to let a long-serving stalwart leave Anfield for free in 2027, according to one insider.

The last player standing from the tail end of Brendan Rodgers’ managerial reign, Joe Gomez is now into his 12th season with the Reds, albeit that he’s been consigned to a backup role thus far under Andoni Iraola.

The 29-year-old has featured for just 259 minutes across our 16 matches so far in this campaign, more than half of which have come in the Carabao Cup (Transfermarkt), and as it stand he’ll be out of contract in seven months’ time.

Ex-Manchester United chief scout Mick Brown has claimed that Liverpool sporting director Julian Ward has already decided that the club’s longest-serving current player won’t be offered a latest deal, with injury issues not helping the defender’s case.

Recent findings suggest that he told Football Insider: “Liverpool have already decided they’re going to let Joe Gomez leave. He doesn’t have much of a role to play at the moment, he’s not starting games at right-back even despite their injuries, and he isn’t competing for a centre-back position.

Sources indicate that “His injuries are always a concern as well. They don’t think he can start games consistently, and all of these challenges stack up eventually.

“It would be a surprise to me if they were to offer him a new contract, especially when you consider they’re going to be looking to bring in new defenders at some stage.

“If he hasn’t played much this season, that’s not going to change with newly introduced players coming in, so I expect he’ll be allowed to look at what other options might be available.”.

In a recent development, want more Empire of the Kop coverage? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for news you can trust.

Ward could be quite busy with contract renewals over the next few months, with Alisson Becker, Virgil van Dijk and Alexis Mac Allister reportedly all in line for prospective new deals.

Whereas that trio are virtually guaranteed to start, though, Gomez usually has to rely on substitute appearances or heavy squad rotation for domestic cup games, and it’s not implausible that he could be allowed to depart on a free transfer next summer.

If that is indeed his fate, he’ll be assured of a raucous send-off at Anfield on the final day of the season, with his popularity among the fan base unmistakably evident by the roar which greeted his successful penalty in the Carabao Cup shootout triumph over Chelsea last month.

As Lewis Steele rightly mentioned, the 29-year-old ‘very rarely puts a foot wrong’ whenever he’s called upon, and even if he isn’t getting much game-time, we don’t doubt that he’s imparting some invaluable advice to the young defenders at Liverpool who can learn so much from him.

Sources indicate that if this is to be Gomez’s last campaign with the Reds, all we ask is that he does finally, finally get his first goal for the club during regulation time. You’d be very hard pressed to find a more popular goalscorer if that moment were to happen!

OpenAI kicked off the GPT-6 generation with Astra in September, then upgraded Sol to GPT-6.1 a few weeks later at DevDay.

Industry observers note that today, GPT-6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol are coming to ChatGPT Work and Codex together. OpenAI says both can finish demanding tasks with fewer output tokens, so you can get more done before hitting your usage limit.

Astra is still the model OpenAI recommends for your hardest projects.

Recent findings suggest that say you have a screenshot of a slide and want the rest of your presentation to look like it. OpenAI says GPT-6.2 Astra can use that screenshot as a template and match the layout, colors, and even the font size.

On the Codex side, OpenAI states Astra is better at making and testing changes in an existing project.

“Early testers reported cleaner code style and more focused tests, with fewer rounds of revision,” OpenAI says.

Sol is the more affordable model for everyday coding and writing, and it gets surprisingly close to Astra on one coding test.

Cognition’s FrontierCode 2.0 measures whether changes to real codebases are good enough for maintainers to merge.

With both models at maximum reasoning effort, OpenAI claims Sol came within half a point of Astra at about one-fifth the cost.

According to recent reports, some of you have been asking very politely. Some of you have just been asking.GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol are now available.Super efficient and built to perform where it counts—the real world.https://t.co/qr2iP0GpfX pic.twitter.com/jLCyVIws2Y.

Both models are available starting today in ChatGPT Work and Codex on Plus, Pro, Enterprise, and Edu.

The $200/month Pro initiative also gets Ultrafast mode for the first time with Sol. The $500/month Pro plan gets Ultrafast on both models, as do eligible Enterprise and Edu workspaces once an admin enables it.

Sources indicate that how fast is Ultrafast? OpenAI states it can generate tokens at up to 4.5 times the standard rate on either model, although it uses more of your allowance. You can switch speeds from the model picker.

Recent findings suggest that developers can use both models through the API today as well. Astra’s standard input and output prices are 20% lower than with GPT-6 Astra, while Sol keeps its GPT-6.1 pricing.

You can read more in OpenAI’s full announcement.

#16832. Claude vs. ChatGPT: 5 key differences that could change which AI you use

AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Tomsguide ↗ Open Full Page

Claude vs. ChatGPT: 5 key differences that could change which AI you use

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1347 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomsguide

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • ChatGPT and Claude are two of the biggest names in AI, and both have become significantly more capable within the last few months.
  • Recent findings suggest that chatGPT has evolved into an all-purpose assistant with tools for everything from image generation and voice conversations to coding and research.
  • I've spent plenty of time testing both, and while there's considerable overlap between what they can do, there are some differences worth understanding before deciding which one deserves your time and money.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

ChatGPT and Claude are two of the biggest names in AI, and both have become significantly more capable within the last few months. Whether you need help writing an email, researching a topic, creating an app or managing your workload, both chatbots can handle far more than simple questions and answers. But despite their similarities, OpenAI and Anthropic have taken different approaches to building their AI assistants.

Recent findings suggest that chatGPT has evolved into an all-purpose assistant with tools for everything from image generation and voice conversations to coding and research. Claude has become hyper-focused on writing, programming and helping users complete more complicated tasks through its growing collection of productivity tools.Now that Anthropic has gone public, people are beginning to wonder what is so special about the company's AI known as Claude.

I've spent plenty of time testing both, and while there's considerable overlap between what they can do, there are some differences worth understanding before deciding which one deserves your time and money.

Here are five of the biggest differences between Claude and ChatGPT.

According to recent reports, claude has developed a reputation for producing natural-sounding text that is especially true for longer pieces. It's also good at following detailed writing instructions and maintaining a consistent tone and style across multiple rounds of editing.

And while ChatGPT is no slouch when it comes to writing, either, it has the advantage of flexibility. You can ask it to rewrite something in five different tones, brainstorm headline ideas or transform a complicated explanation into something a beginner can understand.So, while Claude may be the better starting point for someone writing a novel or polishing a lengthy document, ChatGPT is especially useful when experimenting with different approaches.

Industry observers note that of course, writing quality is subjective. The results also depend on which model you're using and how clearly you explain what you want.

One of ChatGPT's biggest advantages is how many different types of tasks it can handle within the same experience.

According to recent reports, alongside traditional text conversations, ChatGPT supports image generation and editing. You can describe a picture you want to create, upload an existing image to change its appearance or use the chatbot to develop visual concepts.

ChatGPT also offers voice conversations, so people can speak naturally with the assistant instead of typing everything into a chat window.

Claude has expanded its creative capabilities, too, particularly through Artifacts, which lets customers create interactive content, visualizations and applications.

However, Claude's creative tools are more focused on building useful digital experiences than generating standalone images.

For anyone who regularly switches between writing, visual creation and spoken conversations, ChatGPT offers a more versatile experience.

Coding or "vibe coding" has become one of the biggest battlegrounds between Anthropic and OpenAI.

Claude Code is Anthropic's coding agent, designed to work directly with codebases, understand existing projects, make changes and help developers solve complicated programming problems.

It has become particularly popular with developers who want an AI assistant that can work inside their existing development environment.

OpenAI's answer is Codex, which can also navigate repositories, write code, fix bugs and handle development tasks.

Both tools go well beyond generating snippets of code in a chatbot. They can take on larger assignments and work through multiple steps of a project.

The biggest difference is often how developers prefer to work. Claude Code has strong roots in terminal-based development, while Codex offers workflows across different development environments and agent-based tasks.

Industry observers note that for casual owners who occasionally need help building a website or debugging a script, either chatbot can be useful. Developers working on larger projects may find that their preferred coding agent becomes the deciding factor. Personally, I tend to hit my usage limits and blast through tokens faster with Claude Code,.

One of the most interesting changes to Claude is Anthropic's growing focus on turning the chatbot into a coworker.

In a recent development, with Cowork, Claude can take on more complicated assignments involving files, documents and connected tools. Rather than walking through every step in a conversation, users can describe the outcome they want and let Claude work through the assignment.

For example, someone could ask Claude to organize project materials, work through a collection of documents or prepare files for a presentation.

ChatGPT is moving in a similar direction with its own agent capabilities, including ChatGPT Work and Codex.

The difference is how these experiences are organized and presented to customers. Anthropic has emphasized the idea of Claude as a digital coworker that can take responsibility for larger assignments. OpenAI has built a broader ecosystem that includes conversational assistance, research, creative tools and specialized agents.

Neither approach is inherently better, but if you're looking for an AI assistant to do more than answer questions, knowing the difference is notable.

Price is another consideration, particularly if you're not sure how often you'll use an AI chatbot.

Both companies offer free access, although usage limits and available features vary.

ChatGPT Plus and Claude Pro each cost $20 per month in the United States. ChatGPT also offers a lower-priced Go subscription for $8 per month, giving owners another option between the free and Plus tiers.

Claude offers annual billing for Pro, which can reduce the effective monthly cost for users willing to commit to a full year.

In a recent development, of course, usage limits, access to more powerful models and included tools can make one subscription more valuable than another. For example, if you think you're going to be creating more images and want that type of creativity from a model, than you'll want to go with ChatGPT. At the same time, if you're a casual user looking for an affordable upgrade, ChatGPT offers more flexibility in its pricing. But, if you rely heavily on Claude's writing and coding capabilities, Pro may be worth the investment.

It has been revealed that here's some good news: you don't have to choose between one or the other. Because ChatGPT offers so much for free, it might be worth sticking with it. But, if you find yourself going through tokens much faster with Claude, you might want to consider bumping up your subscription to a paid tier. I use both agents for different things, which brings me to another point. The bigger question is what you want your AI assistant to do.

Industry observers note that claude is particularly appealing for people who spend their days writing, coding or working through complicated projects. Its emphasis on natural language and increasingly capable agent tools makes it a strong choice for serious productivity work.

ChatGPT offers a broader experience. Between image generation, voice conversations, research, coding and its growing collection of productivity features, it's designed to serve as an assistant for almost anything.

It has been revealed that if you want one AI chatbot that can handle the widest variety of everyday tasks, start with ChatGPT. If your priorities are writing, coding and managing complex workflows, Claude deserves a serious look. And since both offer free versions, the easiest way to decide is to give them the same five prompts and see which one delivers the results you actually prefer.

For a larger screen and better picture quality, the 65-inch Plus Series Smart TV is down to $429.99 from $649.99, saving you $220. The extra screen space also makes it a better fit for a main living room TV.

You don’t necessarily need a upcoming television to enjoy Roku’s streaming platform, because the 2025 Streaming Stick HD can add it to the TV you already own, and right now, it’s $19, down from $39.99. It draws power from a compatible TV’s USB port and streams in 1080p, making it a good fit for older HD TVs, guest rooms, and even hotel TVs. Read PCMag’s review for more details.

For TVs that support 4K, the Streaming Stick Plus is a step up, offering sharper resolution and support for HDR10 and HDR10+ while keeping the same compact, USB-powered design as the HD model. It supports 4K streaming with HDR10 and HDR10+ and uses two 1.9-inch full-range drivers with a bass port to deliver fuller audio than most built-in TV speakers.

Disney+ ‘Percy Jackson’ season 3 review: Bigger battles, darker mythology and more Percabeth (with some drama)
